method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of the Analects, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Legge 1893; Soothill 1910) and checked against the Classical Chinese; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, book by book.
sourcesCited: Classical Chinese, the original text of the Lunyu (論語)
James Legge, The Chinese Classics, Vol. I (1893, public domain)
W. E. Soothill, The Analects of Confucius (1910, public domain)
D. C. Lau (1979, consulted, not quoted)
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the Analects in plain modern English that keeps the terse, aphoristic weight of Confucius's recorded conversations — learning and ritual, ren (human-heartedness), and becoming fully human — without the Victorian scaffolding.
introduction: The Analects are not a treatise but a scrapbook of sayings and exchanges, set down by students after Confucius's death. They circle a few themes — learning, ritual, family, good government, and the cultivation of a humane character — in brief, often cryptic notes. Read slowly; each line is meant to be turned over.

divergences.older: true virtue; perfect virtue; benevolent actions (Legge)
divergences.lectio: human-heartedness
divergences.note: Legge folds ren into a generic 'virtue,' blurring it with de — virtue as moral force, the word behind 'govern by virtue' in Book II. Ren is the specific excellence of being fully human toward other humans, and it is the book's central word. We render it 'human-heartedness' everywhere and keep 'virtue' for de, so the reader can watch the two ideas move separately.

divergences.older: the superior man; a man of complete virtue (Legge)
divergences.lectio: the gentleman
divergences.note: Legge's 'superior man' reads as rank, and rank is exactly what junzi is not. The word originally meant 'a lord's son'; Confucius remade it to mean a formed character, open to anyone willing to do the work. 'Gentleman' — a man defined by conduct rather than birth — carries that remaking in English.

divergences.older: Parents are anxious lest their children should be sick (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Give your father and mother nothing to worry about except your health
divergences.note: The Chinese is famously compressed — 'parents / only / their sickness / worry' — and can be read as a remark about parents' anxiety or as counsel to the son. Read as counsel, it answers the question that was actually asked, what is filial devotion: live so well that illness is the one worry you ever cause them.

divergences.older: keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Keep the old warm and know the new
divergences.note: Wen is literally 'to warm' — the image is of tending a fire, keeping yesterday's food from going cold. Legge abstracts the image away; we keep the hearth in it.

divergences.older: the rules of propriety (Legge)
divergences.lectio: ritual
divergences.note: Legge's 'rules of propriety' makes li sound like an etiquette code. Li is one living thing — rite, ceremony, and the learned forms that respect takes — and this book is its home ground. Kept as a single word throughout, it lets sayings like 'you love the sheep; I love the rite' land the way the Chinese does.

divergences.older: eight rows of pantomimes (Legge)
divergences.lectio: eight rows of dancers
divergences.note: A yi is a file of eight ritual dancers; eight files of eight — sixty-four — belonged to the son of heaven alone. 'Pantomimes' is Victorian theater-talk that hides the offense: a family of ministers helping themselves to the emperor's rite.

divergences.older: to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others (Legge)
divergences.lectio: loyalty, and putting yourself in the other man's place
divergences.note: The one thread through the Master's Way is two plain words, and Legge unspools them into a philosophy lecture. Zhong is doing your utmost in good faith; shu is measuring what you do to others by what you would have done to you — the practice Tsze-kung is still reaching for in Book V. We keep it the size the Chinese keeps it.

divergences.older: By observing a man's faults, it may be known that he is virtuous (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Look at the faults, and you know the human-heartedness
divergences.note: Legge resolves the aphorism into a claim it does not quite make — that faults prove virtue. The Chinese says only that faults come in kinds, and that reading a man's faults reads his ren. We leave the saying open, as the original leaves it.

divergences.older: I grant you, you are not equal to him (Legge)
divergences.lectio: You and I — neither of us is his equal
divergences.note: Yu can mean 'to grant, agree with' or simply 'and,' so the Master either concedes Tsze-kung's point or joins him in it. Read as 'and,' the teacher steps down beside his student — a warmer reading, long favored by commentators, and truer to how the Master speaks of Hui everywhere else.

divergences.phrase: 斐然成章，不知所以裁之
divergences.older: They are accomplished and complete so far, but they do not know how to restrict and shape themselves (Legge)
divergences.lectio: They weave brilliant cloth, and they do not know how to cut it
divergences.note: The Chinese is a live textile figure — zhang is patterned cloth, cai the tailor's cut. Legge flattens it into abstraction; kept whole, it says exactly what the Master means about his young students: dazzling material, and no shaping hand yet.

divergences.older: There is Yung!— He might occupy the place of a prince.
divergences.lectio: Yung — you could seat him on a throne.
divergences.note: The Chinese says only that Yung 'could be made to face south' — the ruler's seat faced south, so the compass direction is the throne. Legge unpacks the idiom into a hedged office; the Lectio keeps the verdict as blunt as the Master gives it.

divergences.older: When the accomplishments and solid qualities are equally blended, we then have the man of virtue.
divergences.lectio: Polish and substance in balance — that is a gentleman.
divergences.note: Wen is finish — pattern, culture, surface; zhi is the raw stuff underneath. 'Polish' and 'substance' keep the craftsman's metaphor that Legge's abstractions blur, and junzi here is the gentleman, not a 'man of virtue.'

divergences.older: A cornered vessel without corners.— A strange cornered vessel! A strange cornered vessel!
divergences.lectio: A cornered cup with no corners — call that a cornered cup? Call that a cornered cup?
divergences.note: The gu was a ritual drinking cup defined by its corners; by Confucius's day the shape had changed and the name no longer fit the thing. Legge hears bafflement ('strange'); the Chinese is a bitter rhetorical question about words coming apart from realities.

divergences.older: They sought to act virtuously, and they did so; what was there for them to repine about?
divergences.lectio: They sought human-heartedness and found it. What was there to regret?
divergences.note: Legge dissolves ren into generic virtue and loses the ledger-like balance of the sentence: the brothers sought a thing and received exactly that thing. Keeping ren visible keeps the verdict — on Po-i and Shu-ch'i, and by implication on the ruler of Wei — legible.

divergences.older: The subjects on which the Master did not talk, were— extraordinary things, feats of strength, disorder, and spiritual beings.
divergences.lectio: The Master did not speak of marvels, feats of strength, rebellion, or the spirits.
divergences.note: Four bare words in the Chinese, a drumbeat. Luan in this company is political violence — rebellion, subversion — not mere untidiness, and the list should land as bluntly as it was kept.

divergences.phrase: 仁遠乎哉？我欲仁，斯仁至矣
divergences.older: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
divergences.lectio: Is human-heartedness so far away? The moment I want it, it is here.
divergences.note: Three quick clauses in the Chinese, with no cry of wonder; Legge's 'lo!' adds a stage flourish. The point is speed — desire and arrival in the same breath.

divergences.older: straightforwardness, without the rules of propriety, becomes rudeness
divergences.lectio: honesty without ritual is harshness
divergences.note: Jiao is a cord drawn strangling-tight: honesty that bites. Legge's 'rudeness' makes it a lapse of manners; 'harshness' keeps the hurt without adding an image the Chinese does not have, and keeps the saying's run of plain nouns. The warning is that honesty unmeasured by ritual wounds people.

divergences.phrase: 民可使由之，不可使知之
divergences.older: The people may be made to follow a path of action, but they may not be made to understand it.
divergences.lectio: The people can be made to follow the Way; they cannot be made to understand it.
divergences.note: The object is the Way itself, not a generic 'path of action.' Often read as cynicism, the line can as easily be a plain limit of government: practice can be commanded; understanding cannot.

divergences.older: It is not easy to find a man who has learned for three years without coming to be good.
divergences.lectio: Three years of study without a thought of salary — such a man is not easy to find.
divergences.note: Gu is literally 'grain,' the form an official's pay took. Legge follows a reading that turns it into 'goodness'; most translators since take it as pay — the rare student is the one whose study never becomes a career move.

divergences.older: After the death of King Wan, was not the cause of truth lodged here in me?
divergences.lectio: King Wan is dead — but does his culture not live on, here, in me?
divergences.note: Wen is the civilization of Chau — its writing, rites, and music — and the sentence puns on King Wan's own name. Legge's 'cause of truth' gives the passage a missionary ring; what Confucius claims to carry is an inheritance of culture, not a creed.

divergences.older: A youth is to be regarded with respect.
divergences.lectio: Stand in awe of the young.
divergences.note: Wei is fear, awe — the same word used for the decrees of Heaven. The young are a force bearing down on the present, not juniors owed politeness.

divergences.phrase: 三軍可奪帥也，匹夫不可奪志也
divergences.older: The commander of the forces of a large state may be carried off, but the will of even a common man cannot be taken from him.
divergences.lectio: You can carry off the commander of a whole army. You cannot carry off the will of one common man.
divergences.note: The Chinese repeats one violent verb, duo — to seize, to carry off — for both the general and the will. Keeping the same verb in both halves keeps the shock of the comparison.

divergences.older: The superior man did not use a deep purple, or a puce colour, in the ornaments of his dress.
divergences.lectio: He wore no deep purple or puce at his collar and cuffs.
divergences.note: The whole book is an eyewitness inventory of one man's conduct, so junzi here is Confucius observed, not a rule for gentlemen at large. Legge keeps the generic 'superior man'; the Lectio lets the chapter stay what it is — a portrait.

divergences.older: Seeing the countenance, it instantly rises. It flies round, and by and by settles.
divergences.lectio: At the look on their faces, the bird rose; it wheeled, and then settled.
divergences.note: The book's closing lines are broken text — every translator mends them differently. The Lectio keeps the fracture and the mystery: a bird that reads faces and knows its moment, set at the end of a book about a man who did the same.

divergences.phrase: 不患寡而患不均 (bu huan gua er huan bu jun)
divergences.older: not troubled lest their people should be few, but are troubled lest they should not keep their several places
divergences.lectio: does not worry that his people are few; he worries that what they have is shared unevenly
divergences.note: Legge follows commentators who soften jun 均 into everyone 'keeping his place.' The word means evenness of distribution, and the argument that follows — share evenly and there is no poverty — only works if you read it plainly.

divergences.phrase: 蕭牆之內 (xiao qiang zhi nei)
divergences.older: within the screen of their own court
divergences.lectio: inside their own walls
divergences.note: The xiaoqiang is the screen-wall just inside a lord's gate. Confucius's warning is that the Chi family's real danger is domestic, not across the border; 'inside their own walls' keeps the threat where he aimed it.

divergences.phrase: 鄉原，德之賊也 (xiangyuan, de zhi zei ye)
divergences.older: Your good, careful people of the villages are the thieves of virtue
divergences.lectio: The village paragon is the thief of virtue
divergences.note: The xiangyuan is a single figure — the local model of respectability whose counterfeit decency passes for goodness. Legge dilutes the dart into a class of people; the saying is aimed, and it stays singular here.

divergences.older: They show how to regulate feelings of resentment
divergences.lectio: They can teach you how to voice a grievance
divergences.note: Yuan is voiced grievance. Confucius is licensing protest — the Odes give you the words for it — not prescribing self-command. Legge manages the feeling; the original authorizes its expression. 'Voice a grievance' keeps that standing without the pettiness of 'complain.'

divergences.phrase: 鳳兮鳳兮 (feng xi feng xi)
divergences.older: O FANG! O FANG!
divergences.lectio: Phoenix! Phoenix!
divergences.note: Feng is not a name but the sacred bird that appears only when the Way prevails in the world. The madman of Ch'u hails Confucius as a phoenix arrived in the wrong age — Legge's bare transliteration hides the whole taunt.

divergences.phrase: 君子惡居下流 (junzi wu ju xialiu)
divergences.older: the superior man hates to dwell in a low-lying situation, where all the evil of the world will flow in upon him
divergences.lectio: a gentleman hates to live downstream: everything foul in the world comes washing down to him
divergences.note: Xialiu is a river's lower reaches. Tsze-kung's point about the tyrant Chau's reputation is hydraulic — infamy, like water, pools at the lowest point — and 'downstream' keeps the current moving.

divergences.older: O most great and sovereign God
divergences.lectio: most august and sovereign Lord
divergences.note: Legge the missionary rendered Di 帝 with the Christian 'God.' The Lectio keeps T'ang's address to the high Lord of Heaven in its older, formal register without importing a theology the text does not carry.

divergences.phrase: 允執其中 (yun zhi qi zhong)
divergences.older: Sincerely hold fast the due Mean
divergences.lectio: Hold faithfully to the center
divergences.note: Zhong in Yao's charge to Shun is the center line of just judgment — practical balance in ruling — not yet the codified 'Doctrine of the Mean' that Legge's capitalized term suggests to a reader. Yun is truly, faithfully: the charge is to hold to it without wavering, and 'honestly' would read as candor.

divergences.older: this is called injury
divergences.lectio: that is called laying a trap
divergences.note: Zei is harm done by design. The offense — issuing an order casually, then enforcing the deadline without mercy — sets people up to fail; 'laying a trap' names the mechanism where 'injury' only names the wound.

divergences.phrase: 吾與點也 (wu yu Dian ye)
divergences.older: I give my approval to Tien (Legge)
divergences.lectio: I am with Tien.
divergences.note: The Master sighs deeply — 喟然嘆 — and then says three words. Legge turns the sigh's verdict into committee language, an approval granted. Yu is the plain 'with' that joins companions on a road: offered ministries, armies, and temple posts, the old man chooses the river outing, the breeze, and the walk home singing.

divergences.older: they may be called ordinary ministers (Legge)
divergences.lectio: ministers who fill out the ranks
divergences.note: Ju is 'equipment, the full set' — a ju-minister makes up the numbers, a tool in the roster. Legge's 'ordinary' merely grades them; the Chinese shelves them, which is why the Master's one concession — they would not follow an order to kill a father or a prince — lands as hard as it does.

divergences.phrase: 過猶不及 (guo you bu ji)
divergences.older: To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Too far is no better than not far enough.
divergences.note: Four characters balanced on you, 'is like' — the proverb weighs the same on both sides and carries no moral vocabulary at all. Legge's 'wrong' adds a judgment the Chinese leaves to the scales.

divergences.phrase: 克己復禮為仁 (ke ji fu li wei ren)
divergences.older: To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue (Legge)
divergences.lectio: To master yourself and return to ritual — that is human-heartedness.
divergences.note: Every word Legge blurs here is load-bearing. Ke is mastery — self-conquest, not suppression; li is ritual, not an etiquette code's 'propriety'; ren is the book's central word, not generic 'perfect virtue.' And in the next clause the world does not 'ascribe' anything, as in Legge's bookkeeping — tianxia gui ren: the world comes home to human-heartedness, gui the word for returning where one belongs.

divergences.phrase: 己所不欲，勿施於人 (ji suo bu yu, wu shi yu ren)
divergences.older: not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself (Legge)
divergences.lectio: What you do not want done to you, do not do to others.
divergences.note: The negative golden rule, five centuries before its positive twin. Legge folds it into a subordinate clause in a list of duties; in the Chinese it is a free-standing command of eight characters — and it returns word for word in Book XV as the one rule a man can walk with all his life.

divergences.phrase: 君子之德風，小人之德草 (junzi zhi de feng)
divergences.older: The relation between superiors and inferiors, is like that between the wind and the grass (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The virtue of the gentleman is wind; the virtue of the small man is grass.
divergences.note: Legge announces the simile before letting it blow. The Chinese is two flat equations and then the physics: when wind crosses grass, the grass must bend. Government as weather, not as sermon — and the Master's whole answer to a ruler who had just proposed killing people for their own good.

divergences.phrase: 君子和而不同 (he er bu tong)
divergences.older: The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable (Legge)
divergences.lectio: The gentleman is in harmony without being in unison. The small man is in unison without being in harmony.
divergences.note: He and tong are music words: harmony is different notes agreeing; unison is one note doubled. Legge's 'affable' and 'adulatory' move the saying into drawing-room manners and lose the acoustics — the gentleman can differ from you and still accord with you; the small man echoes you and accords with nothing.

divergences.older: the ardent and the cautiously-decided (Legge)
divergences.lectio: the wild and the fastidious
divergences.note: Kuang is real wildness — the overshooters, all reach and no restraint; juan the men so scrupulous there are things they will simply not do. Legge grooms both into respectability, and the confession disappears: the Master will take an extremist of either kind over the lukewarm middle he cannot find.

divergences.phrase: 剛毅木訥近仁 (gang yi mu ne jin ren)
divergences.older: The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest are near to virtue (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Firm, steadfast, plain, and slow of speech — that is close to human-heartedness.
divergences.note: Ne is not modesty; it is the halting tongue, the same trait the Master praises in Book XII's slow speaker — mu is wood-plain, the unvarnished grain. And the target is ren, not generic virtue: four unpolished traits stand nearer the center of the book than eloquence ever gets.

divergences.phrase: 邦有道，穀；邦無道，穀，恥也 (bang you dao, gu)
divergences.older: When good government prevails in a state, to be thinking only of salary; and, when bad government prevails, to be thinking, in the same way, only of salary;— this is shameful (Legge)
divergences.lectio: When the state keeps the Way, draw your pay. When the state has lost the Way, to draw your pay all the same — that is shameful.
divergences.note: Gu is literally 'grain,' the form an official's stipend took, and the Chinese carries no 'thinking only of.' Legge inserts a mental attitude so that both halves come out shameful; read plainly, serving a state that keeps the Way is exactly what pay is for. The shame is staying on the payroll after the Way is gone.

divergences.phrase: 如其仁，如其仁 (ru qi ren)
divergences.older: Whose beneficence was like his? Whose beneficence was like his? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Where is the human-heartedness to match his! Where is the human-heartedness to match his!
divergences.note: The scandal of the verdict is the word itself: Kwan Chung, the arch-pragmatist who did not die for his lord, is credited with ren — because he spared the whole world a war. Legge's 'beneficence' hides the shock of hearing the book's highest word land on its least saintly figure, twice.

divergences.phrase: 知其不可而為之 (zhi qi bu ke er wei zhi)
divergences.older: It is he,— is it not?— who knows the impracticable nature of the times and yet will be doing in them (Legge)
divergences.lectio: the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on doing it
divergences.note: Seven characters from an anonymous gatekeeper, and the most famous description of Confucius ever spoken. Legge pads it into a Victorian mouthful; the Chinese is a plain, devastating epitaph — knows it cannot be done, does it anyway — and the book lets it stand without reply.

divergences.older: Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Would that not be reciprocity?
divergences.note: Asked for one word to walk with for life, the Master offers shu — the word Book IV unpacked as 'putting yourself in the other man's place.' Here it must stay a single word, so the Lectio keeps Legge's 'reciprocity' but takes off his capital letters: the Chinese floats the answer as a guess — 'would it not be shu?' — it does not engrave it. Then comes the eight-character rule from Book XII, word for word.

divergences.phrase: 人能弘道，非道弘人 (ren neng hong dao)
divergences.older: A man can enlarge the principles which he follows; those principles do not enlarge the man (Legge)
divergences.lectio: A man can make the Way great. The Way does not make the man great.
divergences.note: Legge's plural 'principles' dissolves dao into a code of conduct. The saying is about the one Way — and its startling claim that the Way waits on men to carry it and widen it, not the other way around. Eight characters, hinged in the middle; the English should hinge the same way.

divergences.phrase: 民之於仁也，甚於水火 (min zhi yu ren)
divergences.older: Virtue is more to man than either water or fire (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Human-heartedness matters more to the people than water and fire.
divergences.note: The word is ren, not generic virtue — and min, the common people, not 'man.' Water and fire are the two things no household can live a day without; the saying sets ren above them, then turns on the grim joke that of the three, only one has never killed anyone.

books.label: Book I
paragraphs: The Master said, "To learn, and in good time to practice what you have learned — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from far away — is that not a joy? To go unrecognized and feel no bitterness — is that not a gentleman?"

Master Yu said, "Men who honor their parents and respect their elder brothers rarely have a taste for defying their superiors, and no man without that taste has ever been fond of stirring up revolt. The gentleman tends to the root; when the root is set, the Way grows from it. Devotion to parents and respect for elders — surely these are the root of human-heartedness."
The Master said, "Clever words and a winning face rarely keep company with human-heartedness."
Master Tsang said, "Each day I examine myself on three points. Working for others, was I faithless? With my friends, did I fail to keep my word? What was handed on to me, did I leave unpracticed?"
The Master said, "To govern a state of a thousand chariots: attend to the work and keep your word; spend little and love the people; and call on their labor only in the right season."

The Master said, "A young man should be devoted to his parents at home and respectful to his elders away from it. He should be careful and truthful, love everyone, and keep close to the human-hearted. If he has strength left after that, let him spend it on study."

Tsze-hsia said, "A man who prizes worth over beauty, who serves his parents with all his strength, who would give his life for his prince, and whose word to his friends is good — others may say he is unlearned; I will call him learned."

The Master said, "A gentleman without gravity carries no weight, and his learning does not hold. Put loyalty and good faith first. Have no friends who are not your equals. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to change."
Master Tsang said, "Give the dead their full rites, and keep the long-departed in remembrance, and the virtue of the people will grow deep again."

Tsze-ch'in asked Tsze-kung, "Wherever our master goes, he learns everything about how the place is governed. Does he ask for it, or is it offered?" Tsze-kung said, "Our master gets it by being warm, upright, courteous, temperate, and deferential. His way of asking is not other men's way of asking."

The Master said, "While a man's father lives, watch what he means to do. When his father dies, watch what he does. If for three years he does not turn from his father's way, he may be called a devoted son."

Master Yu said, "In the practice of ritual, ease is the thing to prize. This was the beauty of the way of the ancient kings; in matters small and great, they followed it. But there is a limit. To know the worth of ease and be easy, without ritual to give it shape — that will not do either."

Master Yu said, "When a promise keeps close to what is right, you can make your word good. When respect keeps close to ritual, you stay clear of shame. When the man you lean on is the right man to be close to, you can take him for your guide."

The Master said, "A gentleman does not ask that his food be rich or his home be easy. He is quick in his work and careful in his speech, and he goes where men of the Way are, to be set straight by them. Call such a man a lover of learning."

Tsze-kung said, "Poor, but no flatterer; rich, but not proud — what would you say to that?" The Master said, "Good. But not so good as poor and glad, or rich and in love with ritual." Tsze-kung said, "The Book of Poetry says, 'Cut, then file; carve, then polish.' Is that what you mean?" The Master said, "Now I can begin to talk about the odes with Ts'ze. Tell him what came before, and he knows what comes next."
The Master said, "Do not be troubled that men do not know you. Be troubled that you do not know men."
books.title: Learning

books.label: Book II
paragraphs: The Master said, "Govern by virtue, and you are like the north star: it keeps its place, and all the stars turn about it."
The Master said, "The Book of Poetry holds three hundred pieces, and one phrase covers them all: no crooked thoughts."

The Master said, "Lead the people with laws and level them with punishments, and they will dodge the punishment and feel no shame. Lead them with virtue and level them with ritual, and they will feel shame — and set themselves right."

The Master said, "At fifteen, I set my heart on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew Heaven's will. At sixty, my ear was tuned to it. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired without crossing the line."

Mang I asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Never disobey." Later, as Fan Ch'ih was driving him, the Master said, "Mang-sun asked me about filial devotion, and I told him: never disobey." Fan Ch'ih said, "What did you mean by it?" The Master said, "While they live, serve your parents by ritual. When they die, bury them by ritual, and sacrifice to them by ritual."
Mang Wu asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Give your father and mother nothing to worry about except your health."
Tsze-yu asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "Nowadays, filial devotion means keeping one's parents fed. But dogs and horses are kept fed too. Without reverence, where is the difference?"

Tsze-hsia asked about filial devotion. The Master said, "The face is the hard part. When there is work, the young shoulder it; when there is wine and food, the elders are served first — is that all it is to be a devoted son?"

The Master said, "I could talk with Hui all day and he would not once differ with me, as if he were slow. But when he had gone, I watched what he did on his own, and it unfolded what I had taught him. Hui is not slow."
The Master said, "See what a man does. Look into why he does it. Find where he comes to rest. How can a man stay hidden? How can a man stay hidden?"
The Master said, "Keep the old warm and know the new, and you are fit to teach."
The Master said, "A gentleman is not a vessel."
Tsze-kung asked about the gentleman. The Master said, "He acts first. Then his words follow his acts."
The Master said, "The gentleman is broad, not partisan. The small man is partisan, not broad."
The Master said, "Learning without thought is labor lost. Thought without learning is dangerous."
The Master said, "To give your strength to strange doctrines — that is harm indeed."
The Master said, "Yu, shall I teach you what it is to know? When you know a thing, hold that you know it. When you do not, admit that you do not. That is knowing."

Tsze-chang was studying with his eye on a salary. The Master said, "Hear much, set aside what is doubtful, and speak carefully about the rest, and you will seldom be blamed. See much, set aside what is dangerous, and act carefully on the rest, and you will seldom be sorry. Words that draw little blame and acts that leave little regret — the salary lies in that."

Duke Ai asked, "What must I do to make the people submit?" Confucius replied, "Raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and the people will submit. Raise the crooked and set them above the straight, and the people will not submit."

Chi K'ang asked how to make the people reverent and loyal, and eager for virtue. The Master said, "Preside over them with gravity, and they will be reverent. Be a devoted son and a kind master, and they will be loyal. Raise up the good and teach those who fall short, and they will be spurred on."

Someone said to Confucius, "Sir, why do you take no part in government?" The Master said, "The Shu-ching says of filial devotion: 'Be devoted to your parents and a friend to your brothers, and it will carry into government.' That too is governing. Why must a man hold office to govern?"
The Master said, "A man whose word cannot be trusted — I do not know what he is good for. A big cart without a yoke-bar, a small cart without a collar-pin: how do you make them go?"

Tsze-chang asked whether what comes ten generations from now can be known. Confucius said, "The Yin took its rites from the Hsia; what it dropped and what it added can be known. The Chau took its rites from the Yin; what it dropped and what it added can be known. And whoever follows the Chau — though a hundred generations pass, it can be known."
The Master said, "To sacrifice to a spirit that is not your own is flattery. To see what is right and not do it is cowardice."
books.title: Governing

books.label: Book III
paragraphs: Confucius said of the head of the Chi family, who had eight rows of dancers perform in his courtyard, "If he can bear to do this, what can he not bear to do?"

The three families had the Yung ode sung while the sacrificial vessels were cleared. The Master said, "'The princes assist; the son of heaven, deep and grave.' What can those words mean in the hall of the three families?"
The Master said, "A man without human-heartedness — what is ritual to him? A man without human-heartedness — what is music to him?"
Lin Fang asked what comes first in ritual. The Master said, "A great question! In ritual, better spare than lavish. In mourning, better grief than a flawless performance."
The Master said, "The tribes of the east and north still have their princes. They are not like our great land, which goes without."

The head of the Chi family was about to sacrifice to the T'ai mountain. The Master said to Zan Yu, "Can you not save him from this?" He answered, "I cannot." The Master said, "Alas! Will you tell me the T'ai mountain is less discerning than Lin Fang?"

The Master said, "A gentleman has nothing to contend for. If contend he must, let it be at archery: he bows to his rivals and goes up, comes down again and drinks the forfeit. Even in his contending, he is a gentleman."

Tsze-hsia asked, "What do these lines mean — 'The dimples of her artful smile, the clear black and white of her eye, the plain ground for the colors'?" The Master said, "The colors come after the plain ground." "Then ritual comes after?" The Master said, "It is Shang who draws out my meaning. Now I can begin to talk about the odes with him."

The Master said, "I could describe the rites of the Hsia, but Chi cannot bear witness for me. I could describe the rites of the Yin, but Sung cannot bear witness for me. Their records and their wise men are too few. Were they enough, I could call on them to prove my words."
The Master said, "At the great sacrifice, once the opening libation is poured, I have no wish to watch what follows."
Someone asked the meaning of the great sacrifice. The Master said, "I do not know. To the man who knew, the whole kingdom would lie as plain as this" — and he pointed to his palm.

He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present. He sacrificed to the spirits as if the spirits were there. The Master said, "If I am not present at the sacrifice myself, it is as if I had not sacrificed."
Wang-sun Chia asked, "What does the saying mean — 'Better to court the kitchen stove than the southwest corner'?" The Master said, "Not so. A man who sins against Heaven has no one left to pray to."
The Master said, "Chau had two dynasties to look back on. How full, how fine its pattern! I follow Chau."

The Master, entering the grand temple, asked about everything. Someone said, "Who calls the son of the man of Tsau a master of ritual? He enters the grand temple and asks about everything." The Master heard of it and said, "The asking is the ritual."
The Master said, "In archery, piercing the hide is not the point, for men's strength is not equal. That was the old way."
Tsze-kung wanted to do away with the sheep offered at the announcing of each new moon. The Master said, "Ts'ze, you love the sheep. I love the rite."
The Master said, "Serve your prince with the whole of ritual, and men will call it flattery."

Duke Ting asked how a prince should use his ministers, and how ministers should serve their prince. Confucius replied, "The prince uses his ministers according to ritual. The ministers serve their prince with loyalty."
The Master said, "The Kwan Tsu: joy, but never license; grief, but never a wound."

Duke Ai asked Tsai Wo about the altars of the land. Tsai Wo replied, "The sovereigns of Hsia planted them with pine; the men of Yin, with cypress; the men of Chau, with chestnut — to make the people tremble, they said." When the Master heard of it, he said, "What is done, do not discuss. What has run its course, do not contest. What is past, do not blame."

The Master said, "Kwan Chung was a small vessel!" Someone said, "Was Kwan Chung frugal, then?" "Kwan had the San Kwei, and no officer of his did double duty. How is that frugal?" "Then did Kwan Chung know ritual?" The Master said, "The princes of states set a screen before their gates; Kwan set a screen before his too. When two princes met in friendship, they had a stand for the turned-down cups; Kwan had such a stand too. If Kwan knew ritual, who does not know ritual?"

The Master, instructing the grand music-master of Lu, said, "This much of music can be known. It opens with all the parts sounding together. Then, given rein, they run pure and clear, each voice distinct, unbroken — and so to the close."

The border warden at Yi asked to be presented to the Master. "When men of worth have come to this place," he said, "I have never been refused." The followers presented him, and when he came out he said, "Friends, why grieve over your master's fall from office? The world has long been without the Way. Heaven is going to use your master as a bell with a wooden tongue."
The Master said of the Shao music that it was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good, and of the Wu that it was perfectly beautiful, but not perfectly good.
The Master said, "High place without largeness of spirit, ritual without reverence, mourning without grief — what is there for me to look at?"
books.title: Eight Rows of Dancers

books.label: Book IV
paragraphs: The Master said, "It is human-heartedness that makes a neighborhood beautiful. If a man can choose where to live and passes it by, how is he wise?"
The Master said, "Without human-heartedness, a man cannot bear hardship long, and he cannot bear comfort long either. The human-hearted rest in it. The wise know what it is worth."
The Master said, "Only the human-hearted man can rightly love men, and rightly hate them."
The Master said, "Set your will on human-heartedness, and there is no room left for evil."

The Master said, "Riches and rank are what men want; if they cannot be had in the right way, do not hold them. Poverty and low place are what men hate; if they cannot be escaped in the right way, do not escape them. Take human-heartedness from a gentleman, and what is left of the name? A gentleman does not leave it for the length of a meal. In a hurry, he holds to it. In danger, he holds to it."

The Master said, "I have never seen a man who loved human-heartedness, or one who hated its opposite. The lover would set nothing above it. The hater would practice it by letting nothing opposed to it come near him. Is there a man who can give his strength to it for one day? I have never seen one whose strength was too little. If such a man exists, I have not seen him."
The Master said, "A man's faults run true to his kind. Look at the faults, and you know the human-heartedness."
The Master said, "Hear the Way in the morning, and you can die that evening without regret."
The Master said, "A scholar sets his heart on the Way. If he is ashamed of shabby clothes and plain food, he is not worth talking to."
The Master said, "The gentleman moves through the world with nothing fixed for and nothing fixed against. He goes with what is right."
The Master said, "The gentleman thinks of virtue; the small man thinks of comfort. The gentleman thinks of what the law will exact; the small man thinks of what favor he can win."
The Master said, "Act always with an eye to your own advantage, and you will be much resented."
The Master said, "If a man can govern his country by ritual and deference, what difficulty will he have? And if he cannot, what is ritual to him?"
The Master said, "Do not worry that you have no position; worry about what it takes to stand in one. Do not worry that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing."

The Master said, "Shan, one thread runs through my Way." Master Tsang said, "Yes." The Master went out, and the other disciples asked, "What did he mean?" Master Tsang said, "The Master's Way is loyalty, and putting yourself in the other man's place. That is all."
The Master said, "The gentleman is at home in what is right; the small man is at home in what pays."
The Master said, "When you see a worthy man, think how to equal him. When you see an unworthy one, turn and examine yourself."

The Master said, "In serving your parents, you may reason with them — gently. If you see they will not follow, be more reverent still, and do not turn back. And though it wears you out, do not resent them."
The Master said, "While your parents live, do not travel far. If travel you must, have a fixed place to go."
The Master said, "If for three years a son does not turn from his father's way, he may be called a devoted son."
The Master said, "Your parents' years must never be out of mind — at once a joy and a fear."
The Master said, "The ancients were slow to speak. They were ashamed to have their deeds fall short of their words."
The Master said, "Few go wrong by holding back."
The Master said, "The gentleman wants to be slow in his words and quick in his deeds."
The Master said, "Virtue does not stand alone. It always finds neighbors."
Tsze-yu said, "Press your prince too often, and you will be disgraced. Press your friends too often, and they will fall away."
books.title: Human-Heartedness

books.label: Book V
paragraphs: The Master said of Kung-ye Ch'ang that he was fit to be given a wife: he had been in bonds, but the guilt was never his. And he gave him his own daughter in marriage.

Of Nan Yung the Master said that in a well-governed country he would never be out of office, and in an ill-governed one he would keep clear of punishment and disgrace. He gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
The Master said of Tsze-chien, "There is a gentleman! If Lu held no gentlemen, where did this man get it?"
Tsze-kung asked, "And I, Ts'ze — what do you say of me?" The Master said, "You are a vessel." "What kind of vessel?" "A jeweled vessel for the altar."

Someone said, "Yung is human-hearted, but he has no ready tongue." The Master said, "What is a ready tongue for? Meet men with a quick mouth and they will hate you for it, more often than not. Whether Yung is human-hearted I do not know — but why should he need a ready tongue?"
The Master wanted Ch'i-tiao K'ai to take office. He replied, "I cannot yet trust myself so far." The Master was pleased.

The Master said, "The Way makes no headway. I will board a raft and drift out to sea — and the one who follows me will be Yu, I expect." Tsze-lu, hearing it, was glad. The Master said, "Yu loves daring more than I do. But he does not stop to weigh the thing."

Mang Wu asked whether Tsze-lu was human-hearted. The Master said, "I do not know." He asked again, and the Master said, "In a state of a thousand chariots, Yu could be given the levies to manage. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know." "And what of Ch'iu?" The Master said, "In a town of a thousand households, or a house of a hundred chariots, Ch'iu could be made steward. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know." "And what of Ch'ih?" The Master said, "With his sash bound, standing in court, Ch'ih could be set to talk with the guests and visitors. Whether he is human-hearted, I do not know."

The Master said to Tsze-kung, "Which of you is the better, you or Hui?" Tsze-kung replied, "How could I dare look as high as Hui? Hui hears one thing and knows ten. I hear one thing and know two." The Master said, "No, you are not his equal. You and I — neither of us is his equal."

Tsai Yu lay asleep in the daytime. The Master said, "Rotten wood cannot be carved. A wall of dung and mud takes no trowel. Why should I even scold Yu?" The Master said, "There was a time when I heard a man's words and trusted his deeds to match. Now I hear the words and watch the deeds. Yu changed that in me."
The Master said, "I have never seen a man who is truly unbending." Someone answered, "Shan Ch'ang." The Master said, "Ch'ang? Ch'ang is full of desires. How could he be unbending?"
Tsze-kung said, "What I do not want done to me, I want to do to no one." The Master said, "Ts'ze, that is beyond you."
Tsze-kung said, "The Master's culture and conduct — these we are given to hear. What the Master says of our nature and of the Way of Heaven, no one gets to hear."
When Tsze-lu had heard a thing and not yet carried it out, his one fear was hearing another.
Tsze-kung asked, "Why was Kung-wan given the name Wan?" The Master said, "He was quick, and he loved learning, and he was not ashamed to ask those beneath him. That is why they called him Wan."

The Master said of Tsze-ch'an that he had four marks of the gentleman: in his own conduct he was humble; in serving his superiors, respectful; in providing for the people, kind; in commanding them, just.
The Master said, "Yen P'ing knew how to keep a friend. However long he knew a man, his respect was what it had been on the first day."
The Master said, "Tsang Wan housed a great tortoise in a hall of its own, with hills carved on the pillar-tops and duckweed painted on the posts above the beams. What kind of wisdom is that?"

Tsze-chang asked, "The minister Tsze-wan took office three times and showed no pleasure, and was removed three times and showed no resentment — and each time he gave the incoming minister a full account of his government. What do you say of him?" The Master said, "He was loyal." "Was he human-hearted?" "I do not know. Where is the human-heartedness in it?" Tsze-chang went on, "When the officer Ch'ui killed the prince of Ch'i, Ch'an Wan, who owned forty horses, abandoned them and left the country. In the next state, he said, 'They are like our officer Ch'ui here,' and left. He came to a third, said the same, and left again. What do you say of him?" The Master said, "He was clean." "Was he human-hearted?" "I do not know. Where is the human-heartedness in it?"
Chi Wan thought three times before he acted. When the Master heard of it, he said, "Twice is enough."
The Master said, "While the country kept the Way, Ning Wu was wise. When the country lost it, he played the fool. His wisdom can be matched. His folly cannot."
When the Master was in Ch'an, he said, "Home — let me go home! The young men of my school are bold and hasty. They weave brilliant cloth, and they do not know how to cut it."
The Master said, "Po-i and Shu-ch'i did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so the grudges against them were few."
The Master said, "Who calls Wei-shang Kao upright? A man begged vinegar of him, and he begged it from his neighbor and gave it as his own."

The Master said, "Clever words, a winning face, respect laid on thick — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of them, and so am I. To hide a grudge against a man and treat him as a friend — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of that, and so am I."

Yen Yuan and Chi Lu were at his side. The Master said, "Come, why not each of you tell me his wish?" Tsze-lu said, "I would share my chariots and horses and light furs with my friends, and if they wore them to ruin, think nothing of it." Yen Yuan said, "I would never boast of what is good in me, nor parade what I have done." Tsze-lu said, "And now, sir, we would hear your wish." The Master said, "To give the old rest. To keep faith with friends. To cherish the young."
The Master said, "It is hopeless. I have yet to see a man who could look at his own faults and press the case against himself."
The Master said, "In a hamlet of ten houses there is surely someone as loyal and true as I am. But no one who loves learning as I do."
books.title: Weighing Men

books.label: Book VI
paragraphs: The Master said, "Yung — you could seat him on a throne." Chung-kung asked about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. The Master said, "He will do. He keeps things simple." Chung-kung said, "If a man is exacting with himself and simple in what he asks of his people, that is fine. But to be easy on yourself and easy in everything you do — isn't that carrying simplicity too far?" The Master said, "Yung is right."

The Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved to learn. Confucius answered, "There was Yen Hui. He loved to learn. He never took his anger out on the wrong man; he never made the same mistake twice. By ill fortune his allotted time was short, and he died. Now there is no one — I have yet to hear of anyone who loves learning the way he did."

When Tsze-hwa was sent on a mission to Ch'i, the disciple Zan asked for grain for Tsze-hwa's mother. The Master said, "Give her a fu." Zan asked for more. "Give her a yu," said the Master. Zan gave her five ping. The Master said, "When Ch'ih set out for Ch'i, he rode behind sleek horses in light furs. And I have always heard: a gentleman helps the desperate; he does not make the rich richer." When the Master made Yuan Sze governor of his town, he gave him nine hundred measures of grain. Sze declined them. The Master said, "Don't. Could you not give it away — to your neighborhood, your hamlet, your village?"
The Master said of Chung-kung, "If the calf of a brindled ox is red and well-horned, men may hesitate to offer it — but will the spirits of the mountains and rivers refuse it?"
The Master said, "Hui could go three months without his heart once straying from human-heartedness. The others manage a day here, a month there, and no more."

Chi K'ang asked whether Chung-yu was fit for office. The Master said, "Yu is decisive. What trouble would office give him?" "And Ts'ze — is he fit for office?" "Ts'ze sees through things. What trouble would office give him?" "And Ch'iu?" "Ch'iu has many talents. What trouble would office give him?"
The head of the Chi family sent for Min Tsze-ch'ien to be governor of Pi. Min Tsze-ch'ien said, "Decline for me — politely. If anyone comes back a second time, they will find me across the Wan."

Po-niu was sick, and the Master went to see him. Taking his hand through the window, he said, "We are losing him. It is Heaven's decree — and yet, that this man should have this disease! That this man should have this disease!"
The Master said, "What a man Hui was! One bowl of rice, one gourd of water, a hovel in a back lane — no one else could have borne the misery, and it never once touched his joy. What a man Hui was!"

Yen Ch'iu said, "It is not that I take no delight in your Way, Master. I lack the strength." The Master said, "Those who lack the strength give out somewhere along the road. You have drawn your line before setting out."
The Master said to Tsze-hsia, "Be a scholar of the gentleman's kind, not the small man's."

When Tsze-yu was governor of Wu-ch'ang, the Master said, "Have you found any good men?" He answered, "There is Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming. He never takes a shortcut, and he has never once come to my office except on public business."

The Master said, "Mang Chih-fan does not boast. When the army broke and ran, he kept the rear; only as they reached the gate did he whip up his horse, saying, 'It was not courage that kept me back. My horse would not go.'"
The Master said, "Without the glib tongue of the litanist T'o or the good looks of prince Chao of Sung, it is hard to get through in the present age."
The Master said, "Who leaves a house except by the door? Why, then, will no one walk by this Way?"
The Master said, "When substance outweighs polish, you get a rustic. When polish outweighs substance, you get a clerk. Polish and substance in balance — that is a gentleman."
The Master said, "A man is born straight. If he loses that and lives on, he is simply lucky to have escaped."
The Master said, "Those who know it are not the equal of those who love it, and those who love it are not the equal of those who delight in it."
The Master said, "To those above the average, you may speak of the highest things. To those below it, you may not."

Fan Ch'ih asked about wisdom. The Master said, "Give yourself to what is owed to men; respect the spirits, but keep your distance from them. Call that wisdom." He asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "The human-hearted man puts the hard work first and any reward out of mind. Call that human-heartedness."
The Master said, "The wise delight in water; the human-hearted delight in mountains. The wise move; the human-hearted are still. The wise are joyful; the human-hearted live long."
The Master said, "One change, and Ch'i would stand where Lu stands. One change, and Lu would reach the Way."
The Master said, "A cornered cup with no corners — call that a cornered cup? Call that a cornered cup?"

Tsai Wo asked, "Tell a human-hearted man there is a man down the well, and I suppose he jumps in after him?" Confucius said, "Why would he? A gentleman can be sent to the well, but not down it. He can be deceived; he cannot be made a fool of."
The Master said, "A gentleman who studies widely and reins himself in with ritual is not likely to go far wrong."
The Master went to see Nan-tsze, and Tsze-lu was not pleased. The Master swore to him, "If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven throw me aside! May Heaven throw me aside!"
The Master said, "The virtue of the Constant Mean — how complete it is! And how long it has been rare among the people!"

Tsze-kung said, "What about a man who poured out benefits on the people and could help them all — what would you say? Could he be called human-hearted?" The Master said, "Why stop at human-hearted? He would be a sage. Even Yao and Shun fell short of that. The human-hearted man is this: wanting to stand, he helps others to stand; wanting to arrive, he helps others arrive. To take what is near — yourself — as the measure for others: that is the way to human-heartedness."
books.title: Knowing, Loving, Delighting

books.label: Book VII
paragraphs: The Master said, "I transmit; I do not invent. I trust the ancients and I love them. Quietly, I compare myself to our old P'ang."
The Master said, "To store up knowledge in silence, to learn without tiring, to teach without wearing out — which of these can I claim?"
The Master said, "Virtue left untended; learning left undiscussed; hearing what is right and failing to move toward it; being unable to change what is bad in me — these are the things that worry me."
In his leisure hours the Master was easy and unbent, his face open and pleased.
The Master said, "How far I have sunk! How long it has been since I dreamed of the duke of Chau."
The Master said, "Set your heart on the Way. Hold fast to virtue. Lean on human-heartedness. Take your recreation in the arts."
The Master said, "No one has ever come to me with so much as a bundle of dried meat and gone away untaught."

The Master said, "I do not open the door for a man who is not straining at it, or find the word for one who is not struggling to speak. I hold up one corner; if he cannot come back with the other three, I do not go on."
When the Master ate beside a mourner, he never ate his fill. On a day he had wept, he did not sing.

The Master said to Yen Yuan, "When wanted, to serve; when set aside, to withdraw — only you and I have that in us." Tsze-lu said, "If you had command of the armies of a great state, whom would you take with you?" The Master said, "Not the man who would wrestle a tiger bare-handed or wade a river and die with no regrets. The man I take comes to the thing afraid, loves to plan, and carries the plan through."
The Master said, "If wealth could be had for the seeking, I would take up the whip and hold horses to get it. Since it cannot, I will follow what I love."
The things the Master treated with the greatest care were fasting, war, and sickness.
In Ch'i, the Master heard the Shao, and for three months he did not know the taste of meat. "I never imagined," he said, "that music could be made as fine as this."

Yen Yu said, "Is our Master for the ruler of Wei?" Tsze-kung said, "Well — I will ask him." He went in and said, "What sort of men were Po-i and Shu-ch'i?" "Worthies of the old days," said the Master. "Did they regret how it ended for them?" "They sought human-heartedness and found it. What was there to regret?" Tsze-kung came out and said, "Our Master is not for him."
The Master said, "Coarse rice to eat, water to drink, my bent arm for a pillow — there is joy in these things too. Wealth and rank that come by wrong are to me drifting clouds."
The Master said, "Give me a few more years — fifty for the study of the Yi — and I might come through without great faults."
The Master's constant themes were the Odes, the History, and the keeping of ritual. Of these he spoke again and again.

The Duke of Sheh asked Tsze-lu about Confucius, and Tsze-lu gave him no answer. The Master said, "Why didn't you say: he is a man so eager he forgets to eat, so glad he forgets every sorrow, and who has not noticed old age coming on?"
The Master said, "I was not born knowing. I love what is old, and I go after it in earnest."
The Master did not speak of marvels, feats of strength, rebellion, or the spirits.
The Master said, "Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher. I pick out what is good in them and follow it; what is bad, and mend it in myself."
The Master said, "Heaven planted this virtue in me. What can Hwan T'ui do to me?"
The Master said, "Do you think I am hiding something, my friends? I hide nothing from you. There is nothing I do that is not laid open before you. That is who I am."
The Master taught four things: letters, conduct, loyalty, and good faith.

The Master said, "A sage I will never get to see; a gentleman would be enough. A good man I will never get to see; a man of constancy would be enough. But men who have nothing and pose as having, who are empty and pose as full, who are pinched and pose as comfortable — constancy is beyond such men."
The Master angled, but never with a net. He shot, but never at a roosting bird.

The Master said, "There may be men who act without knowing why; I am not one of them. To hear much, choose what is good, and follow it; to see much and hold it in memory — that is the second kind of knowledge."

The people of Hu-hsiang were hard to talk with, so when a boy from there was received, the disciples wondered. The Master said, "I take a man at his coming; I do not answer for what he does when he leaves. Why be so hard? If a man cleans himself to come to me, I receive him clean. I do not vouch for his past."
The Master said, "Is human-heartedness so far away? The moment I want it, it is here."

The minister of crime of Ch'an asked whether the duke Chao knew ritual, and Confucius said, "He knew ritual." When Confucius had withdrawn, the minister beckoned Wu-ma Ch'i forward and said, "I have heard that a gentleman takes no side. Does a gentleman take sides after all? The prince took a wife from the house of Wu — his own surname — and covered it by calling her 'The elder Tsze of Wu.' If that prince knew ritual, who does not?" Wu-ma Ch'i passed this on, and the Master said, "I am a fortunate man. If I make a mistake, someone is sure to know it."
When the Master was with a man who sang well, he would have him sing it again, and then join in.
The Master said, "In letters I am perhaps the equal of other men. As for living as a gentleman lives — carrying out in conduct what he professes — I have not yet arrived."

The Master said, "A sage? A man of human-heartedness? How would I dare? Say only this of me: I work toward it without tiring and teach without wearying — that much and no more." Kung-hsi Hwa said, "And that much is exactly what we students cannot learn to do."

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. The Master said, "Is that done?" Tsze-lu answered, "It is. The Eulogies say, 'Prayer has been made for you to the spirits above and below.'" The Master said, "Then my praying began long ago."
The Master said, "Extravagance breeds arrogance; thrift breeds shabbiness. Better shabby than arrogant."
The Master said, "The gentleman is level and open; the small man is never out from under his cares."
The Master was mild, yet firm; imposing, yet not fierce; respectful, yet at ease.
books.title: The Transmitter

books.label: Book VIII
paragraphs: The Master said, "T'ai-po may be called virtue at its highest. Three times he gave up an empire, and he hid it so well the people could not even find words to praise him."

The Master said, "Respect without ritual is drudgery; caution without ritual is timidity; courage without ritual is disorder; honesty without ritual is harshness. When those in high place are devoted to their own kin, the people stir toward human-heartedness. When old friends are not dropped, the people do not turn cold."

Master Tsang was ill. He called the disciples of his school and said, "Uncover my feet. Uncover my hands. The Odes say, 'Trembling, watchful, as if at the edge of a deep gulf, as if treading on thin ice' — and that is how I have lived. But from this moment, my little ones, I know that I have come through whole."

Master Tsang was ill, and Meng Chang came to ask after him. Tsang said, "When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three things a gentleman holds precious in the Way: in his bearing, to keep far from violence and carelessness; in his face, to keep close to good faith; in his words and tone, to keep far from anything low or false. As for the sacrificial vessels, there are officers to mind them."

Master Tsang said, "Able, yet asking those less able; rich in knowledge, yet asking those with little; having, yet seeming to lack; full, yet counting himself empty; wronged, yet never striking back — I had a friend once who lived this way."

Master Tsang said, "A man you could trust with an orphaned prince, a man you could charge with a state of a hundred li, a man no crisis however great can bend — is that a gentleman? That is a gentleman indeed."

Master Tsang said, "An officer cannot go without breadth and staying power. The load is heavy and the road is long. Human-heartedness is the load he carries — is that not heavy? Only death ends the road — is that not long?"
The Master said, "The Odes wake us. Ritual sets us on our feet. Music finishes the work."
The Master said, "The people can be made to follow the Way; they cannot be made to understand it."
The Master said, "A man who loves daring and resents his poverty will make disorder. So will a man without human-heartedness, if you press your hatred of him too far."
The Master said, "A man might have gifts as fine as the Duke of Chau's — but if he is proud and stingy, the rest is not worth a look."
The Master said, "Three years of study without a thought of salary — such a man is not easy to find."

The Master said, "Hold fast to good faith, love learning, and keep to the good Way until death. Do not enter a state that is tottering; do not stay in one in chaos. When the Way runs in the world, be seen; when it does not, stay hidden. When the Way runs in your own state, be ashamed of poverty and obscurity. When it does not, be ashamed of wealth and honors."
The Master said, "If the office is not yours, its policies are not your business."
The Master said, "When the music master Chih began, and the finale of the Kwan Tsu swelled — how it filled the ear!"
The Master said, "Wild, yet not straight; simple, yet not honest; dull, yet not to be trusted — I do not know what to make of such men."
The Master said, "Learn as if you were chasing what you cannot catch — and afraid, even so, of losing it."
The Master said, "How majestic they were — Shun and Yu held the whole world, and held it as if it were nothing to them."

The Master said, "How great a ruler Yao was! Majestic! Only Heaven is great, and only Yao measured up to it. So vast was his virtue that the people could find no name for it. How majestic his achievements; how brilliant the culture and the institutions he left!"

Shun had five ministers, and the world was in order. King Wu said, "I have ten able ministers." Confucius said, "Talent is hard to find — is the saying not true? Only the age when T'ang and Yu met was richer in it than this of Chau; and of Chau's ten, one was a woman, so the able ministers were nine men. King Wan held two of the empire's three parts and with them still served the house of Yin. The virtue of Chau — call that virtue at its highest."

The Master said, "In Yu I can find no flaw. His own food and drink were plain, but his offerings to the spirits were rich with devotion. His everyday clothes were poor, but his sacrificial cap and apron were beautiful. He lived in a low, mean house, and poured his strength into the ditches and channels. In Yu I can find no flaw."
books.title: A Heavy Load, a Long Road

books.label: Book IX
paragraphs: The Master seldom spoke of profit, or of fate, or of human-heartedness.

A man of the village of Ta-hsiang said, "How great the philosopher K'ung is! His learning is vast — and he has made no name in any one thing." The Master heard of it and said to his disciples, "What shall I take up, then? Charioteering? Archery? I will take up charioteering."

The Master said, "Ritual calls for a cap of linen; nowadays it is silk. That is thrifty, and I follow the crowd. Ritual calls for bowing below the hall; nowadays men bow only at the top of the steps. That is arrogant — and though it sets me against the crowd, I still bow below."
There were four things the Master was wholly free of: assumption, insistence, stubbornness, and self.

In K'wang, the Master feared for his life. He said, "King Wan is dead — but does his culture not live on, here, in me? If Heaven had meant this culture to perish, a latecomer like me would never have been given my share in it. And so long as Heaven does not let it perish, what can the men of K'wang do to me?"

A high officer asked Tsze-kung, "Your Master — surely he is a sage? He can do so many things!" Tsze-kung said, "Heaven has certainly given him without stint; he is close to a sage. And besides, he can do many things." The Master heard of it and said, "Does the officer know me? When I was young, I was poor — that is why I can do so many things, and small things they are. Does a gentleman need many skills? He does not." Lao said, "The Master used to say, 'I was never tried in office — so I learned the crafts.'"
The Master said, "Do I possess knowledge? I do not. But let the plainest man ask me a question in earnest, and empty as it may seem, I knock it open at both ends until I have given him everything."
The Master said, "The phoenix does not come; the river sends forth no chart. It is over with me."

When the Master saw a man in mourning dress, or in the full cap and robes of ceremony, or a blind man, he would rise at their approach, though they were younger than he; and if he had to pass them, he quickened his step.

Yen Yuan sighed and said, "I look up at it, and it is higher. I bore into it, and it is harder. I see it before me, and suddenly it is behind. The Master leads a man on step by step, so skillfully — he has broadened me with learning and gathered me in with ritual. I could not stop now if I wished to. And when I have spent every ability I have, something still stands there, sheer above me. I long to follow it — and there is no way up."

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu set the disciples to act as ministers of a great household. In a remission the Master said, "How long Yu has practiced this fraud! Pretending I have ministers when I have none — whom do I deceive? Do I deceive Heaven? And besides — rather than die in the hands of ministers, would I not sooner die in yours, my friends? A grand burial I may miss; but will I die by the side of the road?"
Tsze-kung said, "Say there is a beautiful gem here. Should I shut it in a case and keep it, or find a good price and sell it?" The Master said, "Sell it! Sell it! But I would wait for the offer."

The Master wanted to go and live among the nine wild tribes of the east. Someone said, "They are crude. How could you?" The Master said, "If a gentleman lived among them, what crudeness would be left?"
The Master said, "Only after I came back from Wei to Lu was the music set right, and the Royal songs and the Praise songs each found their place."

The Master said, "Abroad, to serve the ministers and nobles; at home, to serve father and elder brothers; in the rites of the dead, to spare no effort; and never to be overcome by wine — which of these can I claim?"
Standing by a stream, the Master said, "It all passes like this, does it not? Day and night, it never stops."
The Master said, "I have yet to meet the man who loves virtue the way he loves beauty."

The Master said, "It is like raising a mound: one basket of earth short of done, and if I stop, I am the one who stopped. It is like leveling ground: one basketful tipped in, and if I move forward, I am the one moving."
The Master said, "The one who never flagged while I set a thing before him — that was Hui."
The Master said of Yen Yuan, "What a loss! I watched him advance. I never saw him stop."
The Master said, "There are sprouts that never flower. There are flowers that never fruit."

The Master said, "Stand in awe of the young. How do you know their future will not equal our present? Only when a man is forty or fifty and nothing has been heard of him — then there is nothing left in him to fear."

The Master said, "Words of stern correction — who can refuse to assent to them? But mending your ways is what counts. Words of gentle guidance — who can fail to be pleased by them? But unfolding what they point to is what counts. Pleased, but not unfolding; assenting, but not mending — with such a man there is nothing I can do."
The Master said, "Put loyalty and good faith first. Have no friends who are not your equals. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to change."
The Master said, "You can carry off the commander of a whole army. You cannot carry off the will of one common man."

The Master said, "To stand in a worn-out, hemp-quilted gown beside men dressed in fox and badger, and feel no shame — that is Yu, isn't it? 'Envying none, coveting nothing — how could he do anything but good?'" Tsze-lu took to chanting the lines constantly, until the Master said, "That much, by itself — how could it be enough to be good?"
The Master said, "Only when the year turns cold do you learn that the pine and the cypress are the last to fade."
The Master said, "The wise are never bewildered; the human-hearted, never anxious; the brave, never afraid."
The Master said, "Some men you can study with, but not walk the Way with. Some you can walk the Way with, but not stand firm with. Some you can stand firm with, but not weigh things with."

"The flowers of the aspen-plum flutter and turn. How could I not be thinking of you? But your house is far away." The Master said, "There was no real longing in it. To one who truly longs, what is far?"
books.title: The Passing Stream

books.label: Book X
paragraphs: In his own village, Confucius was unassuming and plain, as if words came hard to him. In the ancestral temple of the prince, and at court, he spoke fully on every point, and carefully.

At court, waiting, he talked with the officers of the lower grade freely and directly; with the officers of the higher grade, mildly and precisely. When the ruler was present, he was reverent to the point of unease — grave, and composed.

When the prince called him to receive a guest, his face changed and his legs seemed to catch beneath him. He bowed left and right to the officers beside him as their places required, his robe hanging even before and behind, and hurried forward, his sleeves spread like a bird's wings. When the guest had gone, he always reported back: "The visitor has stopped looking back."

Entering the palace gate, he drew his body in, as if the gate were too small to admit him. He never stood in the middle of the gateway; passing through, he never trod on the threshold. Passing the ruler's empty place, his face changed and his knees bent, and his words came as if breath could barely carry them. Going up to the hall, he gathered his robe in both hands, bent his body, and held his breath as if he dared not breathe. Coming out, when he had descended one step his face eased into relief; from the bottom of the steps he moved quickly forward, sleeves like wings; and back at his own place, the respectful unease returned.

Carrying his ruler's scepter, he bent as if the weight were too much for him, holding it no higher than hands held for a bow, no lower than hands passing a gift; his face changed, as if in fear, and he dragged his feet as if they were tied to the ground. Presenting the gifts of state, his look was placid. At the private audience after, he was glad and at ease.

He wore no deep purple or puce at his collar and cuffs; even his house clothes held no red or reddish shade. In hot weather he wore a single garment of fine or coarse weave, but always over an inner one. Over lamb's fur he wore black; over fawn's fur, white; over fox's fur, yellow. His informal fur robe was cut long, with the right sleeve short. His sleeping-gown had to be half again the length of his body. At home he sat on the thick furs of fox and badger. Out of mourning, he wore all the ornaments of the girdle. Except for court dress, his under-skirt was cut narrow above and full below. Lamb's fur and a black cap were not worn on visits of condolence. And on the first day of the month he put on his court robes and presented himself at court.
Fasting, he put on the bright, clean garment of plain cloth. Fasting, he changed his food, and moved from the place where he usually sat.

He did not object to rice milled fine, nor to meat minced small. Rice soured by heat or damp he did not eat, nor fish or meat that had spoiled; nothing discolored, nothing foul-smelling, nothing badly cooked, nothing out of season. Meat cut wrong he did not eat, nor a dish without its proper sauce. However plentiful the meat, he never let it outweigh the rice. Only in wine he set no measure — but never drank to confusion. Bought wine and market dried meat he did not touch. Ginger was never absent from his table. He did not eat much. After assisting at the prince's sacrifice, he did not keep the meat overnight; the meat of his own family's sacrifices he kept no more than three days — past three days, it was not to be eaten. Eating, he did not converse; in bed, he did not speak. Though the meal were coarse rice and vegetable broth, he would set a little apart in offering, with a grave, respectful face.
If his mat was not straight, he did not sit.

When the villagers drank together, he left only after the elders with their staffs had gone out. When the villagers held the rites to drive out pestilence, he put on his court robes and stood on the eastern steps.

Sending his compliments to someone in another state, he bowed twice as he saw the messenger off. When Chi K'ang sent him a gift of medicine, he bowed and received it — but said, "I do not know this drug. I dare not taste it."
The stable burned down. Coming back from court, the Master said, "Was anyone hurt?" He did not ask about the horses.

When the prince sent him cooked meat, he straightened his mat and tasted it first, then shared it out. When the prince sent raw meat, he had it cooked and offered it to his ancestors. When the prince sent a living animal, he kept it alive. Dining in attendance on the prince, while the prince made the offering, he tasted every dish first. When he was ill and the prince came to see him, he lay with his head to the east, his court robes spread over him and his sash drawn across them. When the prince's summons came, he set out on foot, not waiting for the carriage to be yoked.
Entering the great ancestral temple of the state, he asked about everything.
When a friend died with no family to turn to, he said, "The burial is mine." A friend's gift — though it were a carriage and horses — received no bow. Only one gift did: the flesh of sacrifice.

In bed he did not lie like a corpse. At home he wore no formal air. At the sight of a man in mourning dress, even a familiar friend, his face changed. At the sight of a man in ceremonial cap, or a blind man, even in his house clothes, he showed them the forms of courtesy. To a man in mourning he bowed over the crossbar of his carriage; he bowed the same way to anyone carrying the registers of the people. Where a feast was set in abundance, his face changed and he rose to his feet. At a sudden clap of thunder, or a violent wind, his face changed.
Mounting his carriage, he stood square and took the mounting-cord. Inside it, he did not look sharply about, he did not talk fast, he did not point.

At the look on their faces, the bird rose; it wheeled, and then settled. The Master said, "The hen-pheasant on the hill bridge — she knows her season! She knows her season!" Tsze-lu made a motion toward it. Three times it sniffed the air, and rose.
books.title: At Home and at Court

books.label: Book XI
paragraphs: The Master said, "The men who came first to ritual and music were countryfolk, they say; the men who came after are accomplished gentlemen. When I have use for ritual and music, I go with the men who came first."

The Master said, "Of all who were with me in Ch'an and Ts'ai, not one still comes to my door." Distinguished for virtue and conduct: Yen Yuan, Min Tsze-ch'ien, Zan Po-niu, and Chung-kung. For speech: Tsai Wo and Tsze-kung. For the work of government: Zan Yu and Chi Lu. For letters: Tsze-yu and Tsze-hsia.
The Master said, "Hui is no help to me. There is nothing I say that does not delight him."
The Master said, "What a devoted son Min Tsze-ch'ien is! No one disputes what his own parents and brothers say of him."
Nan Yung kept returning to the lines about the white scepter stone. Confucius gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.

Chi K'ang asked which of the disciples loved to learn. Confucius answered, "There was Yen Hui — he loved to learn. By ill fortune his allotted time was short, and he died. Now there is no one who loves it as he did."

When Yen Yuan died, his father Yen Lu begged the Master to sell his carriage to buy an outer shell for the coffin. The Master said, "Talented or not, a son is a son. When my own son Li died, he had a coffin and no outer shell. I did not go on foot to buy him one. I have walked behind the great officers, and it was not for me to go on foot."
When Yen Yuan died, the Master cried, "Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!"

When Yen Yuan died, the Master wept for him wildly. His followers said, "Master, this grief is too much." "Too much?" he said. "If I do not grieve past measure for this man, for whom should I grieve?"

When Yen Yuan died, the disciples wanted to give him a grand burial. The Master said, "You may not." They buried him grandly anyway. The Master said, "Hui treated me as his father. I was not allowed to treat him as my son. That was not my doing, my friends. It was yours."

Chi Lu asked about serving the spirits of the dead. The Master said, "You cannot yet serve the living — how will you serve the dead?" He ventured to ask about death. "You do not yet understand life — how will you understand death?"

The disciple Min stood at the Master's side looking mild and precise; Tsze-lu, bold and soldierly; Zan Yu and Tsze-kung, frank and easy. The Master was pleased. "A man like Yu," he said, "will not die a natural death."

Some officials of Lu were going to pull down the Long Treasury and rebuild it. Min Tsze-ch'ien said, "What if it were restored as it stands? Why must it be torn down and made new?" The Master said, "This man seldom speaks. When he does, he hits the mark."
The Master said, "What is Yu's lute doing at my door?" After that the other disciples began to slight Tsze-lu. The Master said, "Yu has climbed to the hall. He has not yet entered the inner rooms."
