Tsze-kung asked which was the better man, Shih or Shang. The Master said, "Shih goes too far; Shang does not go far enough." "Then Shih is the better?" "Too far," said the Master, "is no better than not far enough."

The head of the Chi family was richer than the duke of Chau had ever been, and still Ch'iu gathered taxes for him and piled the wealth higher. The Master said, "He is no disciple of mine. Sound the drum, my little ones, and attack him."
Ch'ai is simple. Shan is slow. Shih is all surface. Yu is rough.

The Master said, "There is Hui — almost there, and often with nothing in his bowl. Ts'ze will not accept what Heaven appoints, and his goods multiply; yet when he reckons, he is right more often than not."
Tsze-chang asked about the way of the good man. The Master said, "He does not walk in other men's footprints. But neither does he enter the sage's inner room."
The Master said, "A man's talk is solid and earnest — so we grant him our approval. But is he a gentleman? Or only a man got up to look grave?"

Tsze-lu asked, "When I hear a thing, should I act on it at once?" The Master said, "Your father and elder brothers are alive — how can you act at once on whatever you hear?" Zan Yu asked, "When I hear a thing, should I act on it at once?" The Master said, "Act on it at once." Kung-hsi Hwa said, "Yu asked whether he should act at once on what he hears, and you said, 'Your father and elder brothers are alive.' Ch'iu asked whether he should act at once on what he hears, and you said, 'Act on it at once.' I am confused, and I venture to ask why." The Master said, "Ch'iu hangs back, so I pushed him forward. Yu has drive enough for two men, so I held him back."
When the Master stood in danger in K'wang, Yen Yuan had fallen behind. When he caught up, the Master said, "I thought you were dead." "While you live," said Hui, "how would I dare to die?"

Chi Tsze-zan asked whether Chung Yu and Zan Ch'iu could be called great ministers. The Master said, "I thought you were going to ask about someone remarkable, and it is only Yu and Ch'iu! A great minister serves his prince by the Way, and when he cannot, he resigns. Yu and Ch'iu you may call ministers who fill out the ranks." "Then they will do whatever they are told?" "To kill a father or a prince," said the Master, "— that they would not do."

Tsze-lu got Tsze-kao made governor of Pi. The Master said, "You are ruining another man's son." Tsze-lu said, "There are people there to govern; there are altars of the land and grain. Why must a man read books before anyone calls him learned?" The Master said, "This is why I hate a ready tongue."

Tsze-lu, Tsang Hsi, Zan Yu, and Kung-hsi Hwa were sitting with the Master. He said, "I am a day or so older than you — forget that for now. You are always saying, 'No one knows us.' Suppose some ruler did know you. What would you do?" Tsze-lu answered first, without pausing: "A state of a thousand chariots, squeezed between great powers, armies rolling over it, and famine on top of the war — give it to me, and in three years I could make its people brave, and show them which way to face." The Master smiled at him. "Ch'iu, what about you?" Ch'iu answered, "A territory of sixty or seventy li square, or fifty or sixty — give it to me, and in three years I could give the people plenty. As for ritual and music, that must wait for a gentleman." "And you, Ch'ih?" Ch'ih answered, "I do not say I could do these things; I would want to learn them. At the services of the ancestral temple, and when the princes meet in audience, I should like to put on the dark robe and the black linen cap and serve as a minor assistant." Last of all the Master asked Tsang Hsi: "Tien, what about you?" Tien let the last notes thin away, set his lute aside with a clang of strings, and rose. "My wish is different from anything these three have said." "What harm in that?" said the Master. "Each of us is only telling his wish." Then Tien said, "In the last month of spring, in the new clothes of the season, with five or six young men just capped and six or seven boys, I would bathe in the I, take the breeze at the rain altars, and walk home singing." The Master gave a long sigh and said, "I am with Tien." When the three others had gone out, Tsang Hsi stayed behind and said, "What did you think of what they said?" The Master said, "Each simply told his wish." "Why did you smile at Yu?" "A state is governed by ritual. His words did not yield an inch — that is why I smiled." "But was it not a state that Ch'iu asked for?" "Show me a territory of sixty or seventy li, or fifty or sixty, that is not a state." "And was it not a state that Ch'ih asked for?" "Ancestral temples and audiences of the princes — whose business are they but rulers'? And if Ch'ih is to be a minor assistant there, who could be the major one?"
books.title: Men of Former Times

books.label: Book XII
paragraphs: Yen Yuan asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "To master yourself and return to ritual — that is human-heartedness. Master yourself for one day and return to ritual, and the whole world will come home to human-heartedness. And its practice — does it start from a man himself, or from others?" Yen Yuan said, "May I ask the steps?" The Master said, "Look at nothing against ritual. Listen to nothing against ritual. Say nothing against ritual. Make no move against ritual." Yen Yuan said, "Slow as I am, let me make these words my business."

Chung-kung asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "Away from home, carry yourself as if receiving a great guest. Employ the people as if attending a great sacrifice. What you do not want done to you, do not do to others. Then there will be no resentment against you in the state, and none in the family." Chung-kung said, "Slow as I am, let me make these words my business."

Sze-ma Niu asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "The human-hearted man is slow to speak." "Slow to speak — is that all human-heartedness is?" The Master said, "The doing is hard. Can the saying be anything but slow?"

Sze-ma Niu asked about the gentleman. The Master said, "The gentleman has no anxiety and no fear." "No anxiety, no fear — is that all a gentleman is?" The Master said, "He looks inward and finds nothing to be sick over. What is there to be anxious about? What is there to fear?"

Sze-ma Niu said sorrowfully, "Other men all have brothers. I alone have none." Tsze-hsia said to him, "I have heard this: death and life are decreed; wealth and honors rest with Heaven. Let the gentleman be reverent and leave nothing undone, respectful to others and observant of ritual, and everyone within the four seas is his brother. Why should a gentleman grieve that he has no brothers?"

Tsze-chang asked what it is to be clear-sighted. The Master said, "Slander that soaks in like water, accusations that sting like a wound in the flesh — the man on whom they do not work, call him clear-sighted. The man on whom they do not work at all — call him far-sighted."

Tsze-kung asked about government. The Master said, "Enough food, enough arms, and the people's trust in their ruler." Tsze-kung said, "If it cannot be helped, and one of the three must go, which goes first?" "The arms." "And if it cannot be helped, and one of the remaining two must go?" "The food. Death has been with us from the oldest days. But without the people's trust, nothing stands."

Chi Tsze-ch'ang said, "Substance is all a gentleman needs. What is polish for?" Tsze-kung said, "A pity, sir, to hear a gentleman talk so — a team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue. Polish is substance; substance is polish. Take the hair off a tiger's hide or a leopard's, and it might as well be the hide of a dog or a goat."

Duke Ai asked Yu Zo, "The year is lean, and the revenue does not cover the spending. What should I do?" Yu Zo answered, "Why not take the tithe — one part in ten?" "With two parts in ten I have not enough. How would I manage with one?" Yu Zo answered, "When the people have plenty, how can their prince alone be in want? When the people are in want, how can their prince alone have plenty?"

Tsze-chang asked how to raise virtue higher and how to see through delusion. The Master said, "Put loyalty and good faith first, and keep moving toward what is right — that raises virtue. You love a man, and want him to live; you hate him, and want him dead. To want him alive and want him dead — that is delusion. 'Not indeed for her wealth — and yet you make the change.'"

Duke Ching of Ch'i asked Confucius about government. Confucius answered, "Let the prince be a prince, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son." "Good!" said the duke. "For truly, if the prince is no prince, the minister no minister, the father no father, and the son no son, then though I have my grain, will I live to eat it?"
The Master said, "The man who could settle a lawsuit on half a word — that is Yu!" Tsze-lu never slept on a promise.
The Master said, "At hearing lawsuits I am no better than the next man. What matters is to bring it about that there are no lawsuits."
Tsze-chang asked about government. The Master said, "Keep it before you without tiring. Carry it out with loyalty."
The Master said, "A gentleman who studies widely and reins himself in with ritual is not likely to go far wrong."
The Master said, "The gentleman helps what is fine in men to completion; he does not help what is ugly in them. The small man does the opposite."
Chi K'ang asked Confucius about government. Confucius answered, "To govern is to set straight. Lead the way straight yourself — then who will dare to be crooked?"
Chi K'ang, troubled by thieves, asked Confucius what to do about them. Confucius answered, "If you yourself did not covet, sir, they would not steal though you paid them for it."

Chi K'ang asked Confucius about government, saying, "Suppose I kill the lawless for the good of the law-abiding — what of that?" Confucius answered, "You are governing, sir. What do you need killing for? Want the good, and the people will be good. The virtue of the gentleman is wind; the virtue of the small man is grass. When the wind crosses the grass, the grass must bend."

Tsze-chang asked, "What must an officer be like to be called a man of distinction?" The Master said, "What do you mean by distinction?" "To be heard of through the state; to be heard of through his clan." "That is renown," said the Master, "not distinction. The man of distinction is straight in his substance and loves what is right. He weighs men's words and reads their faces, and he takes care to put himself below others. Such a man is distinguished in the state, and distinguished in his clan. The man of renown puts on the look of human-heartedness while his conduct runs the other way, and he lives in the pose and never doubts it. Such a man will be heard of through the state — and heard of through his clan."

Fan Ch'ih, walking with the Master below the rain altars, said, "May I ask how to raise virtue higher, how to mend hidden faults, and how to see through delusion?" The Master said, "A good question! Put the work first and the reward after — does that not raise virtue? Attack your own evil, and not the evil in others — does that not mend hidden faults? For one morning's anger to forget yourself, and your parents with you — is that not delusion?"

Fan Ch'ih asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "Love men." He asked about knowledge. The Master said, "Know men." Fan Ch'ih did not follow. The Master said, "Raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight." Fan Ch'ih withdrew, and finding Tsze-hsia he said, "Just now I was with the Master and asked him about knowledge. He said, 'Raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight.' What did he mean?" Tsze-hsia said, "How rich a saying! When Shun had the kingdom, he chose from among all the people and raised up Kao-yao — and men without human-heartedness went far away. When T'ang had the kingdom, he chose from among all the people and raised up I Yin — and men without human-heartedness went far away."
Tsze-kung asked about friends. The Master said, "Counsel them in good faith and guide them well. If it is no use, stop. Do not disgrace yourself for them."
Master Tsang said, "The gentleman gathers friends by culture, and by his friends builds up his human-heartedness."
books.title: Yen Yuan

books.label: Book XIII
paragraphs: Tsze-lu asked about government. The Master said, "Go ahead of the people, and work hard for them." He asked for more, and was told, "Never tire."

Chung-kung, then steward to the head of the Chi family, asked about government. The Master said, "Put your officers to their proper work first, pardon small faults, and raise up the worthy and able." "How shall I recognize the worthy and able, to raise them?" "Raise the ones you know. The ones you do not know — will other men leave them aside?"

Tsze-lu said, "The ruler of Wei is waiting for you to run his government. What will you do first?" The Master said, "The one thing needed is to set names right." "So that is it!" said Tsze-lu. "How impractical you are! Why should names need setting right?" The Master said, "How uncouth you are, Yu! On what he does not understand, a gentleman keeps a careful silence. If names are not right, what is said does not answer to what is. If what is said does not answer to what is, nothing can be carried through. When nothing can be carried through, ritual and music do not flourish. When ritual and music do not flourish, punishments miss the mark. And when punishments miss the mark, the people have nowhere to set hand or foot. So the gentleman gives no name that cannot be rightly spoken, and says nothing that cannot be carried out. In his words, the gentleman leaves nothing to carelessness. That is all."

Fan Ch'ih asked to be taught farming. The Master said, "An old farmer would serve you better than I." He asked to be taught gardening. "An old gardener would serve you better than I." When Fan Ch'ih had gone out, the Master said, "What a small man Fan Hsu is! Let those above love ritual, and no one among the people will dare to be irreverent. Let them love what is right, and no one will dare to disobey. Let them love good faith, and no one will dare to deal falsely. Do that, and people will come from every quarter with their children strapped to their backs. What does he need to know about farming?"

The Master said, "A man may have the three hundred Odes by heart; but give him a post in government and he flounders, send him abroad on a mission and he cannot answer for himself — then what use is all his learning?"
The Master said, "When the ruler himself is straight, things go forward without an order given. When he himself is not straight, he may give orders, but no one will follow them."
The Master said, "The governments of Lu and Wei are brothers."

The Master said of Ching, a son of the ducal house of Wei, that he knew how to keep a household. When he first had anything, he said, 'It will just about do.' When he had a little more, he said, 'It is just about complete.' When he was rich, he said, 'It is just about fine.'

When the Master traveled to Wei, Zan Yu drove his carriage. The Master said, "How the people have multiplied!" Yu said, "Once they are many, what more should be done for them?" "Make them rich." "And once they are rich, what more?" "Teach them."
The Master said, "If any ruler would employ me, in twelve months I would have something to show. In three years, the thing would be done."
The Master said, "'If good men governed a state for a hundred years running, cruelty would be overcome and killing done away with.' How true that saying is!"
The Master said, "Even with a true king, it would still take a generation before human-heartedness prevailed."
The Master said, "If a man sets his own conduct straight, what difficulty will he have in governing? If he cannot set himself straight, what business has he setting others straight?"

The disciple Zan came back late from court. The Master said, "Why so late?" "There was government business." The Master said, "Family business, more likely. If there had been government business, I would have heard of it — out of office as I am."

Duke Ting asked whether there is a single saying that can make a state prosper. Confucius answered, "No saying can do quite so much. But there is one that men have: 'To be a prince is hard; to be a minister is not easy.' If a ruler knows how hard it is to be a prince, is that not close to one saying making a state prosper?" "And is there a single saying that can ruin a state?" Confucius answered, "No saying can do quite so much. But there is one that men have: 'I take no pleasure in being a prince — except that no one crosses a word I say.' If his words are good and no one crosses them, well and good. But if they are not good and no one crosses them, is that not close to one saying ruining a state?"
The Duke of Sheh asked about government. The Master said, "Make the near glad, and the far will come."

Tsze-hsia, then governor of Chu-fu, asked about government. The Master said, "Do not want it fast. Do not look at small gains. Want it fast, and you never arrive. Look at small gains, and great things go undone."

The Duke of Sheh told Confucius, "Among us there are men upright to the letter. If a father steals a sheep, the son will bear witness against him." Confucius said, "Our upright men are different. The father covers for the son, and the son covers for the father. There is uprightness in that."
Fan Ch'ih asked about human-heartedness. The Master said, "At home, be courteous. At work, be careful. With others, be loyal. Even among the wild tribes, these are not to be set aside."

Tsze-kung asked, "What must a man be before he deserves to be called an officer?" The Master said, "He keeps a sense of shame about his own conduct, and sent to any quarter, he does not disgrace his prince's commission. That deserves the name." "May I ask about the rank below?" "His kinsmen call him a devoted son; his neighbors call him a good brother." "And the rank below that?" "His word is always kept, his acts always carried through — hard little stones of men. Still, they might make the next rank." "And the men in government today?" The Master said, "Pah — peck-measures and rice-baskets. Not worth the counting."
The Master said, "Since I cannot find men of the middle way to work with, I must have the wild and the fastidious. The wild press forward and take hold; the fastidious have things they will not do."

The Master said, "The people of the south have a saying: 'A man without constancy cannot make even a shaman or a doctor.' It is a good one. And the Changes say, 'Inconstant in his virtue — someone will hand him disgrace.'" The Master said, "For such a man, there is no need of the oracle at all."
The Master said, "The gentleman is in harmony without being in unison. The small man is in unison without being in harmony."

Tsze-kung asked, "What of a man whom everyone in his village loves?" The Master said, "Not enough." "What of a man whom everyone in his village hates?" The Master said, "Not enough either. Better the man whom the good of the village love and the bad of the village hate."

The Master said, "The gentleman is easy to serve and hard to please. Try to please him by any crooked path, and he is not pleased; and when he employs men, he measures them to their capacity. The small man is hard to serve and easy to please. Try to please him, crooked path or not, and pleased he is; and when he employs men, he expects each one to be good at everything."
The Master said, "The gentleman is at ease without arrogance. The small man is arrogant without ease."
The Master said, "Firm, steadfast, plain, and slow of speech — that is close to human-heartedness."

Tsze-lu asked, "What must a man be before he deserves to be called a scholar?" The Master said, "Earnest, encouraging, and warm — that deserves the name. With his friends, earnest and encouraging; with his brothers, warm."
The Master said, "Let a good man teach the people for seven years, and they would be fit even to bear arms."
The Master said, "To send people to war untaught is to throw them away."
books.title: Setting Names Right

books.label: Book XIV
paragraphs: Hsien asked what is shameful. The Master said, "When the state keeps the Way, draw your pay. When the state has lost the Way, to draw your pay all the same — that is shameful."

"When the love of winning, boasting, resentment, and greed are all held down — may that be called human-heartedness?" The Master said, "It may be called difficult. Whether it is human-heartedness, I do not know."
The Master said, "A scholar who hankers after his comforts does not deserve the name of scholar."
The Master said, "When the state keeps the Way, speak boldly and act boldly. When the state has lost the Way, act boldly still — but let your speech go softly."

The Master said, "A man of virtue will always have something to say. A man with something to say does not always have virtue. A human-hearted man will always have courage. A brave man does not always have human-heartedness."

Nan-kung Kwo put a question to Confucius: "The archer I and Ao, who could drag a boat over dry land — neither of them died a natural death. Yu and Chi worked the fields with their own hands — and the kingdom came to them." The Master gave no answer. When Nan-kung Kwo had gone out, the Master said, "There is a gentleman! There is a man who prizes virtue!"
The Master said, "Gentlemen who lack human-heartedness — those there have been. But a small man with human-heartedness — never."
The Master said, "Can you love a man and not make him labor? Can you be loyal to a man and not teach him?"

The Master said, "In the drawing up of a state paper, P'i Shan made the rough draft, Shi-shu examined and discussed it, Tsze-yu, the master of embassies, polished it, and Tsze-ch'an of Tung-li gave it its finish."

Someone asked about Tsze-ch'an. The Master said, "A generous man." He asked about Tsze-hsi. "That man! That man!" He asked about Kwan Chung. The Master said, "He was a man: Pien, a town of three hundred households, was taken from the head of the Po family for him, and the Po chief, brought down to coarse rice, never let one resentful word be heard to the end of his life."
The Master said, "To be poor without resentment is hard. To be rich without arrogance is easy."
The Master said, "Mang Kung-ch'o would make a fine elder for the house of Chao or Wei; but he could not serve as a great officer of Tang or Hsieh."

Tsze-lu asked what makes a complete man. The Master said, "Take the knowledge of Tsang Wu-chung, the freedom from greed of Kung-ch'o, the bravery of Chwang of Pien, and the many talents of Zan Ch'iu, and finish them with ritual and music — that might be called a complete man." Then he said, "But need a complete man of these days have all that? A man who at the sight of gain thinks of what is right; who at the sight of danger is ready to give his life; who does not forget the promise of years ago, however long the years — he too may be called a complete man."

The Master asked Kung-ming Chia about Kung-shu Wan: "Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not take?" Kung-ming Chia answered, "Whoever told you that told you too much. My master speaks when it is time to speak, so no one tires of his speaking. He laughs when there is something to be glad of, so no one tires of his laughing. He takes when taking is right, so no one tires of his taking." The Master said, "So? Can it really be so?"
The Master said, "Tsang Wu-chung held the city of Fang while he asked the duke of Lu to appoint his heir. Say what you like about his not coercing his prince — I do not believe it."
The Master said, "Duke Wan of Tsin was crafty and not straight. Duke Hwan of Ch'i was straight and not crafty."

Tsze-lu said, "When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Shao Hu died with his master. Kwan Chung did not. Was that not a failure of human-heartedness?" The Master said, "That Duke Hwan could gather all the princes together, and not by war-chariots and weapons — that was Kwan Chung's strength. Where is the human-heartedness to match his! Where is the human-heartedness to match his!"

Tsze-kung said, "Kwan Chung was no human-hearted man, surely? When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Kwan Chung could not even die with him — he went on to serve as Hwan's prime minister." The Master said, "Kwan Chung served as minister to Duke Hwan, made him chief of all the princes, and set the whole kingdom in order — and the people are living on his gifts to this day. But for Kwan Chung, we would be wearing our hair loose and buttoning our coats on the left. Would you have him keep the small good faith of a common man and his wife — strangled in some ditch, and no one ever the wiser?"
Kung-shu Wan's own steward, the great officer Hsien, rose to the prince's court at Wan's side. When the Master heard of it, he said, "He deserved to be called Wan."

The Master was speaking of the misrule of Duke Ling of Wei, and Chi K'ang said, "If he is such a man, how is it he does not lose his state?" Confucius said, "Chung-shu Yu looks after his guests and envoys, the litanist T'o keeps his ancestral temple, and Wang-sun Chia commands his army. With officers like those, how should he lose his state?"
The Master said, "Say a thing without a blush, and you will find it hard to make the thing good."

Chan Ch'ang murdered Duke Chien of Ch'i. Confucius bathed, went to court, and told Duke Ai, "Chan Hang has slain his sovereign. I ask you to punish him." The duke said, "Tell the chiefs of the three families." Confucius withdrew, saying, "Because I walk behind the great officers, I did not dare not to speak. And my prince says, 'Tell the chiefs of the three families.'" He went and told the chiefs, and they refused. Confucius said, "Because I walk behind the great officers, I did not dare not to speak."
Tsze-lu asked how to serve a ruler. The Master said, "Never deceive him. And stand up to his face."
The Master said, "The gentleman works his way upward. The small man works his way down."
The Master said, "The men of old learned for their own sake. The men of today learn for the eyes of others."

Chu Po-yu sent a man to Confucius with his greetings. Confucius sat with him and asked, "What is your master working at?" The messenger answered, "My master wants to make his faults fewer, and has not yet managed it." When he had gone out, the Master said, "There is a messenger! There is a messenger!"
The Master said, "If the office is not yours, its policies are not your business."
Master Tsang said, "The gentleman's thoughts do not wander from his post."
The Master said, "The gentleman is ashamed to let his words outrun his deeds."

The Master said, "The Way of the gentleman has three parts, and I can manage none of them: human-hearted, he is never anxious; wise, never bewildered; brave, never afraid." Tsze-kung said, "Master, you have just described yourself."
Tsze-kung was always measuring men against one another. The Master said, "Ts'ze must be a worthy man indeed. I have no time to spare for that."
The Master said, "I am not troubled that men do not know me. I am troubled by my own want of ability."
The Master said, "Not to expect deceit, not to imagine bad faith — and yet to be the first to sense them when they come: is that not a worthy man?"

Wei-shang Mau said to Confucius, "Ch'iu, what is all this perching here and roosting there? Have you become a smooth talker?" Confucius said, "I would not dare to be a smooth talker. But I hate a man who will not budge."
The Master said, "A ch'i is not called a great horse for its strength, but for its virtue."
Someone said, "What do you say of repaying injury with kindness?" The Master said, "Then what will you repay kindness with? Repay injury with straight justice. Repay kindness with kindness."

The Master said, "No one knows me — alas!" Tsze-kung said, "Why do you say no one knows you?" The Master said, "I do not rail at Heaven. I do not blame men. I learn from what is lowest and reach toward what is highest. And the one who knows me — is that not Heaven?"

Kung-po Liao slandered Tsze-lu to Chi-sun. Tsze-fu Ching-po brought word of it, saying, "My master's mind is certainly being poisoned by Kung-po Liao — but I still have power enough to see Liao's corpse exposed in the market and the court." The Master said, "If the Way is to go forward, that is the decree. If the Way is to fall, that is the decree too. What can Kung-po Liao do against the decree?"
The Master said, "Some worthy men withdraw from the world. Some withdraw from a state. Some withdraw at a look. Some withdraw at a word."
The Master said, "Seven men have done so."
Tsze-lu passed a night in Shih-man. The gatekeeper asked, "From whom do you come?" "From Mr. K'ung." "Ah," said the gatekeeper, "the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on doing it?"

One day in Wei the Master was playing the stone chimes, when a man carrying a straw basket passed the door and said, "There is a heart still full of the world, in that beating of stones!" Then he added, "But how petty, that stubborn clang-clang! If no one knows you, give it up, and be done. 'Where the water is deep, wade through in your clothes; where it is shallow, hitch them up.'" The Master said, "How resolute! Giving up — there is nothing hard in that."

Tsze-chang said, "The Book of History says that Kao-tsung kept the royal mourning three years without speaking. What does that mean?" The Master said, "Why single out Kao-tsung? The ancients all did the same. When a sovereign died, the officers of state gathered their duties and answered to the prime minister for three years."
The Master said, "When those above love ritual, the people are easy to lead."

Tsze-lu asked about the gentleman. The Master said, "He cultivates himself with reverent care." "Is that all?" "He cultivates himself, and others find rest in him." "Is that all?" "He cultivates himself, and the whole people find rest in him. He cultivates himself, and the whole people find rest — even Yao and Shun found that past their strength."

Yuan Zang sat sprawled on his heels, waiting for the Master, who said to him, "Young, and never modest; grown, and nothing to your name; old, and refusing to die — you are a pest." And he rapped him on the shin with his staff.

A boy of the village of Ch'ueh used to carry messages between the Master and his visitors. Someone asked about him: "Coming along well, I suppose?" The Master said, "I have seen him take a grown man's seat, and I have seen him walk abreast of his elders. He is not after progress. He is in a hurry to be finished."
books.title: Hsien Asked

books.label: Book XV
paragraphs: Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius about the ordering of troops. Confucius answered, "Matters of sacrificial vessels I have heard something of. Matters of armies I have never studied." The next day he took his leave. In Ch'an the provisions ran out, and his followers grew too sick to stand. Tsze-lu came to him with his anger showing: "So the gentleman, too, can be brought to this?" The Master said, "A gentleman holds firm in want. A small man in want runs over like flood water."

The Master said, "Ts'ze, you take me for a man who has studied much and holds it all in memory?" "Yes," he answered. "Is it not so?" "No," said the Master. "I have one thread, and everything is strung on it."
The Master said, "Yu, the men who know virtue are few."
The Master said, "If any man governed without governing, it was Shun. What did he do? He composed himself in reverence and sat facing due south — that is all."

Tsze-chang asked how a man should act, that his way be open wherever he goes. The Master said, "Let his words be loyal and true, his conduct earnest and careful, and his way will be open even in the lands of the wild tribes, south or north. Let his words be disloyal and false, his conduct careless and cold — will his way be open even in his own district? Standing, see these two things ranged in front of you. Riding, see them leaning on the yoke. Then your way will be open." Tsze-chang wrote the words on his sash.

The Master said, "Straight — that was the historian Yu! When the state kept the Way, he was an arrow. When the state lost the Way, he was an arrow. And a gentleman — that is Chu Po-yu! When the state keeps the Way, he serves. When the state loses it, he can roll his Way up and put it away inside his coat."
The Master said, "To fail to speak with a man worth speaking to is to waste the man. To speak with a man not worth speaking to is to waste your words. The wise waste neither men nor words."

The Master said, "The scholar with a purpose, the man of human-heartedness — they will not cling to life at the cost of human-heartedness. There are times when they will give up their lives to make human-heartedness whole."

Tsze-kung asked how to work at human-heartedness. The Master said, "A craftsman who wants his work good sharpens his tools first. Whatever state you live in, serve the worthiest of its great officers, and make friends with the most human-hearted of its scholars."

Yen Yuan asked how a state should be run. The Master said, "Keep the calendar of Hsia. Ride the plain state carriage of Yin. Wear the ceremonial cap of Chau. For music, the Shao and its dances. Banish the tunes of Chang, and keep clever talkers at a distance — the tunes of Chang are wanton, and clever talkers are dangerous."
The Master said, "A man who gives no thought to what is far off will find his sorrow near at hand."
The Master said, "It is hopeless! I have yet to meet the man who loves virtue the way he loves beauty."
The Master said, "Did Tsang Wan not hold his post like a thief? He knew the worth of Hui of Liu-hsia, and did not raise him to stand at his side in court."
The Master said, "Demand much of yourself, and little of others, and resentment will keep its distance."
The Master said, "A man who never asks himself, 'What am I to make of this? What am I to make of this?' — I can make nothing of him."
The Master said, "Together the whole day, their talk never once touching what is right, and delighting in little feats of cleverness — hard cases indeed!"
The Master said, "What is right is the gentleman's substance. Ritual is how he carries it out, humility is how he brings it forward, good faith is how he completes it. That is a gentleman."
The Master said, "The gentleman is pained by his own want of ability. He is not pained that men do not know him."
The Master said, "The gentleman dreads leaving the world with his name unspoken."
The Master said, "The gentleman makes his demands of himself. The small man makes his demands of others."
The Master said, "The gentleman holds his ground, and does not wrangle. He keeps company, and joins no faction."
The Master said, "The gentleman does not raise a man up because of his words, and he does not throw away words because of the man."
Tsze-kung asked, "Is there one word a man could walk with all his life?" The Master said, "Would that not be reciprocity? What you do not want done to you, do not do to others."

The Master said, "Of the men I deal with, whom do I blame beyond his due, and whom do I praise beyond it? If I have ever praised a man too high, he had been put to the proof first. It was with this same people that the three dynasties kept to the straight road."
The Master said, "I am old enough to remember when a scribe would leave a blank where he was unsure, and a man with a horse would lend it to a neighbor to ride. Now even that much is gone."
The Master said, "Clever words throw virtue into confusion. Impatience in a small thing throws a great plan into ruin."
The Master said, "When the crowd hates a man, look into it. When the crowd loves a man, look into it."
The Master said, "A man can make the Way great. The Way does not make the man great."
The Master said, "To have a fault and not mend it — that is what deserves to be called a fault."
The Master said, "I have gone a whole day without food and a whole night without sleep, to think. It came to nothing. Better to learn."

The Master said, "The gentleman lays his plans for the Way, not for his food. Plow, and hunger can lie in the middle of it; learn, and pay can lie in the middle of it. The gentleman worries about the Way. He does not worry about being poor."

The Master said, "What wisdom reaches, human-heartedness must hold; otherwise, though a man gains it, he will lose it again. What wisdom reaches and human-heartedness holds, he must preside over with dignity, or the people will not respect him. And what wisdom reaches, human-heartedness holds, and dignity presides over, he must still set in motion by ritual. Short of that, it is not yet good."
The Master said, "The gentleman cannot be read in small things, but he can be trusted with great ones. The small man cannot be trusted with great things, but he can be read in small ones."

The Master said, "Human-heartedness matters more to the people than water and fire. I have seen men die from stepping into water and fire. I have never seen a man die from stepping into human-heartedness."
The Master said, "When it comes to human-heartedness, do not yield place — not even to your teacher."
The Master said, "The gentleman is firm in the right; he is not blindly bound by his word."
The Master said, "In serving your prince, be exacting about the work. Let the pay come after."
The Master said, "In teaching, there are no classes of men."
The Master said, "Men whose Ways are different cannot make plans together."
The Master said, "Words are for reaching the meaning. That is all."

Mien, the music-master, came to call. When they reached the steps, the Master said, "Here are the steps." When they reached the mat, the Master said, "Here is the mat." When everyone was seated, the Master told him, "So-and-so is here. So-and-so is there." After the music-master had gone, Tsze-chang asked, "Is that the way to speak with a music-master?" The Master said, "Yes. That is exactly how one helps the blind."
books.title: One Word to Walk With

books.label: Book XVI
paragraphs: The head of the Chi family was about to attack Chwan-yu. Zan Yu and Chi-lu came to see Confucius and said, "Our chief is going to move against Chwan-yu." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, isn't this your failure? Long ago a former king gave the ruler of Chwan-yu charge of the sacrifices to the eastern Mang. Besides, the place lies inside our own borders, and its lord is a minister of the sovereign himself. What business has your chief attacking it?" Zan Yu said, "Our master wants this. Neither of us, his two ministers, wants it." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, Chau Zan had a saying: 'Show your strength and take your place in the ranks; if you cannot, step down.' What good is a guide who won't steady the blind man when he totters, or lift him when he falls? And besides, what you say is wrong. When the tiger or the rhinoceros breaks out of its cage, when the tortoise-shell or the jade is smashed inside its case — whose fault is that?" Zan Yu said, "But Chwan-yu is strong now, and close to Pi. If our chief does not take it today, it will be a grief to his sons and grandsons." Confucius said, "Ch'iu, a gentleman hates the man who will not say plainly 'I want it,' and has to dress the wanting up in reasons. Here is what I have heard: the lord of a state, the head of a house, does not worry that his people are few; he worries that what they have is shared unevenly. He does not worry about poverty; he worries about unrest. For share evenly, and there is no poverty; live in harmony, and there is no lack of people; keep the peace, and nothing gets overthrown."

"And so, if people far away will not submit, you cultivate learning and virtue to draw them in — and once they have come, you give them peace. Now look at the two of you, Yu and Ch'iu, standing at your chief's side. People far away will not submit, and you cannot draw them in. The state itself is splitting and crumbling, and you cannot hold it together. And in the middle of this, he plans to raise spears and shields inside his own country. I am afraid the trouble of the Chi-sun family is not coming from Chwan-yu. It is waiting inside their own walls."

Confucius said, "When the Way holds in the world, ritual, music, and military campaigns issue from the Son of Heaven. When the Way is lost, they issue from the princes — and once they issue from the princes, few houses last ten generations. Once they issue from the great officers, few last five. Once the stewards of the great officers hold the orders of state in their hands, few last three. When the Way holds in the world, government does not sit with the great officers. When the Way holds in the world, the common people do not argue politics."

Confucius said, "The revenue left the ducal house five generations ago. The government has sat with the great officers for four. That is why the descendants of the three Hwan are fading away." Confucius said, "Three friendships profit a man, and three do him harm. Friendship with the upright, friendship with the faithful, friendship with the widely informed — these profit him. Friendship with the man of studied airs, friendship with the practiced flatterer, friendship with the glib — these do him harm."

Confucius said, "Three pleasures profit a man, and three do him harm. Pleasure in the measured practice of ritual and music, pleasure in speaking well of others, pleasure in having many worthy friends — these profit him. Pleasure in extravagance, pleasure in idle roaming, pleasure in the feast — these do him harm." Confucius said, "In attendance on a gentleman, there are three mistakes. To speak before it is your turn — that is called rashness. To hold back when it is your turn — that is called hiding. To speak without reading his face — that is called blindness."

Confucius said, "There are three things a gentleman guards against. In youth, before the blood has settled, he guards against lust. In his prime, when the blood is at full strength, he guards against fighting. In old age, when the blood has thinned, he guards against greed." Confucius said, "There are three things a gentleman stands in awe of. He stands in awe of Heaven's decrees. He stands in awe of great men. He stands in awe of the words of the sages. The small man does not know Heaven's decrees, and so does not fear them. He takes liberties with great men. He makes jokes of the words of the sages."

Confucius said, "Those born knowing it stand highest. Those who learn it and come to know stand next. Those who find it hard and learn anyway come after them. Those who find it hard and do not learn — they are the lowest of the people." Confucius said, "A gentleman keeps nine things in mind. Seeing, he thinks: is it clear? Hearing: is it exact? His expression: is it warm? His bearing: is it respectful? His words: are they true? His work: is it careful? In doubt, he thinks of asking. In anger, he thinks of the trouble to come. And at the sight of gain, he thinks of what is right."

Confucius said, "'They see the good and chase it as if they could never catch up; they see the bad and flinch as if they had put a hand in boiling water' — I have seen the men, and I have heard the words. 'They live hidden to pursue their aims; they do what is right to carry their Way through' — I have heard the words. I have not seen the men." The duke Ching of Ch'i had a thousand teams of four horses; the day he died, the people could not find one virtue to praise him for. Po-i and Shu-ch'i starved to death at the foot of Shau-yang mountain, and the people praise them to this day. Isn't that what the saying means?

Ch'an K'ang asked Po-yu, "Have you heard anything from your father that the rest of us have not?" Po-yu answered, "No. Once, when he was standing alone and I hurried across the courtyard, he said to me, 'Have you learned the Odes?' 'Not yet,' I said. 'If you do not learn the Odes,' he said, 'you will have nothing to say.' I went away and studied the Odes."

"Another day he was standing alone again, and as I hurried across the courtyard he said to me, 'Have you learned ritual?' 'Not yet,' I said. 'If you do not learn ritual,' he said, 'you will have nothing to stand on.' I went away and studied ritual. Those two things are all I have ever heard from him." Ch'an K'ang came away delighted. "I asked one thing," he said, "and I have gotten three. I have heard about the Odes. I have heard about ritual. And I have heard that a gentleman keeps his own son at arm's length."

The wife of the ruler of a state: the ruler calls her Fu Zan, the Lady. She calls herself Hsiao T'ung, this little child. The people of the state call her Chun Fu Zan, our lord's Lady; to people of other states, they speak of her as K'wa Hsiao Chun, our poor little prince. And the people of other states call her Chun Fu Zan as well.
books.title: The Chi Family

books.label: Book XVII
paragraphs: Yang Ho wanted to see Confucius, and Confucius would not see him. So Ho sent him a suckling pig — and Confucius, picking an hour when Ho was out, went to his house to return thanks. But he met him on the road. Ho said to Confucius, "Come here. I want a word with you. A man hides his treasure in his coat while his country loses its way — would you call him human-hearted?" "No," said Confucius. "A man longs to serve, yet over and over lets his moment slip — would you call him wise?" "No," said Confucius. "The days and months are running out. The years do not wait for us." Confucius said, "True. I will take office."
The Master said, "By nature men are close to one another. By habit they end up far apart." The Master said, "Only two kinds never change: the wisest, and the dullest."

The Master came to Wu-ch'ang and heard strings and singing all through the town. He smiled. "Why use an ox-cleaver," he said, "to kill a chicken?" Tsze-yu answered, "Master, I once heard you say, 'When the gentleman studies the Way, he loves men. When the common man studies the Way, he is easy to lead.'" The Master said, "My friends, Yen is right. What I said was a joke." Kung-shan Fu-zao, holding the city of Pi in revolt, sent for the Master, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu didn't like it. "If there is nowhere to go, then do not go," he said. "Why must it be Kung-shan?"

The Master said, "Would the man have called me for nothing? If someone would only use me — could I not make an eastern Chau?" Tsze-chang asked Confucius about human-heartedness. Confucius said, "To be able to carry five things everywhere under heaven — that is human-heartedness." He asked what they were. "Gravity, generosity, good faith, diligence, kindness. Be grave, and no one will treat you with contempt. Be generous, and you will win everyone. Keep faith, and men will trust you with things. Be diligent, and you will get things done. Be kind, and you will be able to ask men for their work."

Pi Hsi sent for him, and the Master was inclined to go. Tsze-lu said, "Master, I once heard you say, 'A gentleman does not walk into the house of a man who has chosen evil with his own hands.' Pi Hsi is holding Chung-mau in revolt. If you go to him, what will people say?" The Master said, "Yes, I said that. But don't they also say: what is truly hard, grinding cannot thin? What is truly white, black dye cannot darken? Am I a bitter gourd, fit to hang on a string and never be eaten?"

The Master said, "Yu, have you heard of the six words and the six faults that shadow them?" "I have not." "Sit down, and I will tell you. To love human-heartedness without loving learning ends in folly. To love knowledge without loving learning ends in drift. To love good faith without loving learning ends in damage. To love straight speech without loving learning ends in harshness. To love courage without loving learning ends in disorder. To love firmness without loving learning ends in recklessness."

The Master said, "My young friends, why does none of you study the Odes? The Odes can rouse you. They can open your eyes. They can put you in company. They can teach you how to voice a grievance. Near at hand, they teach you to serve your father; further off, to serve your prince. And from them you learn the names of birds and beasts, plants and trees, more than you can count." The Master said to Po-yu, "Have you worked through the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan? A man who has not worked through the Chau-nan and the Shao-nan stands with his face against a wall."

The Master said, "'Ritual! Ritual!' they say. Is it jade and silk they mean? 'Music! Music!' they say. Is it bells and drums?" The Master said, "A stern face over a weak heart — set that man among the small men: isn't he the thief who bores through the wall, or climbs over it?" The Master said, "The village paragon is the thief of virtue." The Master said, "To hear it on the road and tell it on the road is to throw virtue away."

The Master said, "These vulgar men — can you serve a prince beside them? Before they have a thing, their one worry is getting it. Once they have it, their one worry is losing it. And a man in dread of losing his place will do anything. There is nothing he will not do." The Master said, "The ancients had three faults, and even those we may have lost. The wild men of old ignored the small things; the wild men of today just run loose. The proud men of old had sharp corners; the proud men of today have sharp tempers. The fools of old were at least straight; the fools of today are simply liars."

The Master said, "Clever words and a winning face rarely keep company with human-heartedness." The Master said, "I hate purple for stealing the place of vermilion. I hate the tunes of Chang for fouling the music of the Ya. I hate the sharp-tongued for toppling states and houses." The Master said, "I would rather say nothing at all." Tsze-kung said, "But Master, if you say nothing, what will we, your students, have to pass on?" The Master said, "Does Heaven say anything? The four seasons turn, the hundred creatures are born — and does Heaven say a word?"

Zu Pei asked to see Confucius, and Confucius sent word that he was ill. Then, as the messenger was going out the door, he took up his lute and sang — making sure Pei heard it. Tsai Wo asked about the three years' mourning for parents. "One year is long enough," he said. "If a gentleman lets ritual alone for three years, ritual will fall apart. If he lets music alone for three years, music will collapse. Within a year the old grain is gone and the new grain is standing; the fire-drill has gone through its round of woods. A year, and mourning should end." The Master said, "A year on — eating fine rice, wearing brocade — would you be at ease?" "I would," said Wo.

"If you are at ease, then do it. A gentleman in mourning tastes no sweetness in fine food, hears no pleasure in music, finds no rest in his own house. So he does not do these things. But you are at ease — so do them." Tsai Wo went out, and the Master said, "There is no human-heartedness in Yu. A child is three years old before it leaves its parents' arms; the three years' mourning is kept everywhere under heaven. And Yu — did he not get his three years of love from his father and mother?"

The Master said, "Stuffed with food to the end of the day, mind set on nothing — a hard case! Are there no dice players, no players of go? Even that would be better than nothing." Tsze-lu said, "Does the gentleman put courage first?" The Master said, "The gentleman puts rightness first. A great man with courage and no rightness makes a rebel. A small man with courage and no rightness makes a robber." Tsze-kung said, "Does the gentleman have his hatreds too?" The Master said, "He has his hatreds. He hates those who broadcast other men's faults. He hates the man beneath who slanders the men above. He hates courage without ritual. He hates the bold and decisive whose minds are shut."

Then the Master asked, "Ts'ze, do you have your hatreds?" Tsze-kung said, "I hate prying passed off as wisdom. I hate insolence passed off as courage. I hate informing passed off as honesty." The Master said, "Women of the house and servants are the hardest to deal with. Come close, and they lose respect. Keep back, and they resent you." The Master said, "If a man is forty and still disliked, that is how he ends."
books.title: Yang Ho

books.label: Book XVIII
paragraphs: The Viscount of Wei withdrew from the court. The Viscount of Chi became a slave to the tyrant Chau. Pi-kan protested, and died for it. Confucius said, "The Yin had three human-hearted men."

Hui of Liu-hsia was chief judge, and three times he was thrown out of office. Someone said, "Isn't it time, sir, to leave altogether?" He said, "If I serve men by the straight Way, where can I go that they will not throw me out three times? And if I am willing to serve men by the crooked way, why should I have to leave the country of my father and mother at all?" The duke Ching of Ch'i, considering how to receive Confucius, said, "I cannot treat him as I would the head of the Chi family. I will treat him as something between Chi and Mang." Then he said, "I am old. I cannot use him." And Confucius left. The people of Ch'i sent Lu a gift of women musicians. Chi Hwan accepted them, and for three days no court was held. And Confucius left.

Chieh-yu, the madman of Ch'u, went past Confucius singing: "Phoenix! Phoenix! How your virtue has withered! What is gone is past all pleading; what is coming can still be caught. Enough, enough! Danger, now, for those who serve in government!" Confucius got down from his carriage, wanting to speak with him. But Chieh-yu quickened his step and was gone, and Confucius could not speak with him. Ch'ang-tsu and Chieh-ni were plowing together in the same field when Confucius passed by, and he sent Tsze-lu to ask them where the ford was. Ch'ang-tsu said, "Who is that, holding the reins?" "That is K'ung Ch'iu," said Tsze-lu. "K'ung Ch'iu of Lu?" "Yes." "Then he knows the ford."

Tsze-lu asked Chieh-ni instead. "And who are you?" said Chieh-ni. "Chung Yu." "The disciple of K'ung Ch'iu of Lu?" "I am." "The whole world is one rushing flood, and who is there to change it with? You follow a master who runs from this man and that man. Wouldn't you do better following men who have run from the world itself?" And he went on raking earth over the seed without a pause. Tsze-lu went back and reported it. The Master fell quiet a moment, then said, "A man cannot flock with the birds and beasts. If I am not to live among these people — among men — whom am I to live with? If the Way held in the world, I would not be out here trying to change it."

Tsze-lu, traveling behind the Master, had fallen back when he met an old man carrying a weeding basket slung on his staff. Tsze-lu asked him, "Sir, have you seen my master?" The old man said, "You, whose four limbs have never worked, who couldn't tell the five grains apart — whose master?" And he planted his staff and went to weeding. Tsze-lu stood and waited, hands folded in respect. The old man kept him for the night, killed a chicken and cooked millet for him, and presented his two sons. Next day Tsze-lu caught up and told the story. The Master said, "A recluse," and sent him back to see the man again. When Tsze-lu got there, the man had gone.

Tsze-lu said to the household, "It is not right to refuse to serve. The courtesies between old and young cannot be set aside; how then can the duty between ruler and minister be set aside? To keep his own person clean, he lets the great relation fall into ruin. A gentleman takes office because it is right to serve — knowing perfectly well that the Way is not going to prevail." The men who withdrew from the world: Po-i, Shu-ch'i, Yu-chung, I-yi, Chu-chang, Hui of Liu-hsia, Shao-lien. The Master said, "Never bending their wills, never letting their persons be shamed — that was Po-i and Shu-ch'i."

"Of Hui of Liu-hsia and Shao-lien you can say they bent their wills and let their persons be shamed. But their words held the line, and their acts were what men hope for. That much, and no more. Of Yu-chung and I-yi you can say they lived hidden and said whatever they pleased. But they kept their persons clean, and their withdrawal weighed the times exactly. I am different from all of them. Nothing is ruled in for me, and nothing is ruled out." Chih, the grand music master, went to Ch'i. Kan, who played at the second meal, went to Ch'u. Liao, of the third meal, went to Ts'ai. Chueh, of the fourth, went to Ch'in. Fang-shu the drummer crossed north of the River.

Wu, who played the hand drum, crossed the Han. Yang the assistant master and Hsiang, who struck the stone chimes, crossed the sea to the islands. The duke of Chau said to his son, the duke of Lu: "A true prince does not neglect his own kin. He does not leave his great ministers bitter at never being used. He does not cast off men of the old families without grave cause. And he does not demand from any one man a talent for everything."
Chau had its eight officers: Po-ta and Po-kwo, Chung-tu and Chung-hwu, Shu-ya and Shu-hsia, Chi-sui and Chi-kwa.
books.title: The Viscount of Wei

books.label: Book XIX
paragraphs: Tsze-chang said, "A scholar in service who, seeing danger, will give his life; who, seeing gain, thinks of what is right; who in sacrifice thinks of reverence and in mourning thinks of grief — he will do." Tsze-chang said, "Holding virtue without breadth, trusting the Way without depth — what does such a man add to the world? And what does he take from it?"

The disciples of Tsze-hsia asked Tsze-chang about making friends. Tsze-chang said, "What does Tsze-hsia tell you?" They answered, "Tsze-hsia says: keep company with those who are worth it, and turn away those who are not." Tsze-chang said, "That is not what I was taught. A gentleman honors the worthy and makes room for the many; he praises the good and pities the incapable. If I am greatly worthy, who is there I cannot make room for? If I am unworthy, men will turn me away first — what business have I turning others away?" Tsze-hsia said, "Even the minor paths have things worth seeing along them. But follow them far and you bog down — which is why the gentleman does not take them."

Tsze-hsia said, "A man who learns, day by day, what he still lacks, and month by month does not lose what he has — call him a lover of learning." Tsze-hsia said, "Study widely and hold your purpose fast; question closely and think about what is near at hand. Human-heartedness is in that." Tsze-hsia said, "The hundred craftsmen live in their shops to finish their work. The gentleman learns, to carry his Way to its end."

Tsze-hsia said, "The small man always dresses up his faults." Tsze-hsia said, "The gentleman changes three times. From far off he looks stern. Up close, he is warm. And when you hear him speak, every word is exact." Tsze-hsia said, "The gentleman wins his people's trust, and then he puts them to work; without the trust, they would call it oppression. He wins his prince's trust, and then he speaks against his faults; without the trust, the prince would call it slander." Tsze-hsia said, "In the great virtues a man must not cross the line. In the small ones, a little coming and going is allowed."

Tsze-yu said, "The students of Tsze-hsia can sprinkle and sweep a floor, answer a call, come forward and step back — and do it well. But those are twigs. Of the root they know nothing. What sort of learning is that?" Tsze-hsia heard it and said, "Ah, Yen Yu is wrong. In the gentleman's Way, which lesson do you hand on first? Which do you leave to ripen? Students are like plants: you tend each kind as its kind requires. The gentleman's Way does not cheat its beginners. And to hold it whole, first things and last things in a single grasp — only the sage does that."

Tsze-hsia said, "Strength left over from office should go to learning. Strength left over from learning should go to office." Tsze-hsia said, "Mourning should go all the way to grief, and stop there." Tsze-hsia said, "My friend Chang can do what other men find nearly impossible. Even so, he is not yet human-hearted." Master Tsang said, "How grand Chang is! Hard to work at human-heartedness beside a man like that." Master Tsang said, "I heard this from the Master: no man ever gives the whole of himself — unless it is in mourning his parents."

Master Tsang said, "I heard this from the Master: the filial piety of Mang Chwang — in most of it, other men could match him. But he changed nothing: his father's ministers, his father's way of governing, he kept them all. That is the part hard to match." The head of the Mang family made Yang Fu a criminal judge, and Yang Fu came to Master Tsang for advice. Tsang said, "The men above have lost the Way, and the people have come apart — and it has been so for a long time. When you dig out the truth of a case, grieve for them and pity them. Never congratulate yourself on finding it."

Tsze-kung said, "The tyrant Chau cannot have been as wicked as his name. This is why a gentleman hates to live downstream: everything foul in the world comes washing down to him." Tsze-kung said, "The faults of a gentleman are eclipses of the sun and moon. When he fails, everyone sees it. When he mends it, everyone looks up again." Kung-sun Ch'ao of Wei asked Tsze-kung, "Where did Chung-ni get his learning?" Tsze-kung said, "The Way of Wan and Wu has not fallen to the ground yet. It is alive in people. The worthy remember its great parts; the rest remember its small ones. Nobody is without a piece of the Way of Wan and Wu. Where could our Master go and not be learning? And why should he have needed one fixed teacher?"

Shu-sun Wu-shu said to the great officers at court, "Tsze-kung is a better man than Chung-ni." Tsze-fu Ching-po repeated it to Tsze-kung, who said, "Put it in terms of a house and its wall. My wall comes up to a man's shoulder: anyone walking by can look over and see whatever is good inside. The Master's wall is many fathoms high: unless you find the gate and enter, you will never see the beauty of the ancestral temple or the hundred officers in their splendor. And the ones who find the gate, I think, are few. So the chief's remark — what else would you expect?"

Shu-sun Wu-shu spoke against Chung-ni. Tsze-kung said, "Save your breath. Chung-ni cannot be pulled down. The worth of other men is a hill, a mound — a thing you can still climb over. Chung-ni is the sun and the moon. There is no climbing over them. A man may choose to shut them out, but what harm does that do the sun and the moon? It only shows how badly he has measured himself." Ch'an Tsze-ch'in said to Tsze-kung, "You are being modest. In what way is Chung-ni better than you?" Tsze-kung said, "One word can mark a gentleman wise, and one word can mark him a fool. We cannot afford to be careless in what we say. No one reaches the Master, the way no one climbs a stairway to the sky."

"Had the Master been given a state or a great house, it would have gone as the old words say. He plants the people, and they stand. He leads them, and they walk. He settles them, and they come from every side. He stirs them, and they move as one. Living, he is their glory. Dead, he is their grief. How could anyone reach him?"
books.title: Tsze-chang

books.label: Book XX
paragraphs: Yao said, "Ah, Shun. The count of Heaven's succession rests now on your shoulders. Hold faithfully to the center. If the four seas fall into hardship and want, Heaven's gift ends forever." Shun laid the same charge on Yu. T'ang said, "I, the little child Li, dare to offer this dark bull, and dare to declare it plainly to you, most august and sovereign Lord: the guilty I dare not pardon; your servants I do not hide from you. The judging of them is in your own heart, Lord. If there is guilt in me, let it not touch the ten thousand regions. If there is guilt in the ten thousand regions, let it rest on me."

Chau gave great gifts, and good men grew rich. "I have kinsmen of my own," said the king, "but better than kinsmen are human-hearted men. If the hundred families do wrong, let it lie on me — the One Man." He set the weights and measures right, went over the laws again, restored the officers who had been dismissed — and government flowed through the whole kingdom. He raised up states that had been wiped out, mended lines of succession that had been cut, called back to office men who had gone into hiding — and the hearts of everyone under heaven turned to him. What he gave most weight to: the people's food, mourning, and sacrifice. He was generous, and won the crowd. He kept faith, and the people leaned on him. He was diligent, and the work was done. He was just, and they were glad.

Tsze-chang asked Confucius, "What must a man do, to be fit to govern?" The Master said, "Let him honor the five fine things and cast out the four ugly things. Then he is fit to govern." Tsze-chang said, "What are the five fine things?" The Master said, "The gentleman in authority is generous without expense. He works the people, and they do not resent it. He desires, and is not greedy. He is at his ease, and is not proud. He is imposing, and never fierce."

Tsze-chang said, "What is 'generous without expense'?" The Master said, "Benefit the people by way of the things that already benefit them — generous, is it not, and at no expense? Choose the labors that are rightly theirs and set them to work — who resents that? Desire human-heartedness, and obtain human-heartedness — where is the greed in that? Many or few, great or small, the gentleman never dares to brush a man aside — at ease, is he not, and never proud? He sets his robe and cap straight and lifts a level gaze, and men look at him with awe — imposing, is he not, and never fierce?" Tsze-chang said, "And the four ugly things?" The Master said, "To execute people without ever teaching them — that is called cruelty. To demand the finished count without fair warning — that is called tyranny. To let an order lie slack and then insist on it to the day — that is called laying a trap."

"And when a thing must be given to men in any case, to count it out grudgingly — that is called playing the petty clerk." The Master said, "A man who does not know Heaven's decree has no way to be a gentleman. A man who does not know ritual has no way to stand. A man who does not know words has no way to know men."
books.title: Yao Said
